runs.text: I feel stripped. I feel cold. Is this my punishment for letting my voice be heard by men? Oh, I
need to open my eyes first.
Lottie opens her eyes to a world full of color. "SHE'S AWAKE!" someone yells.
A hand brushes against her own, soothing the pain shooting up her spine.
"Darling, we found you unconscious under that old bridge. Are you feeling alright now?" an old,
warm-looking woman asks with concern.
Lottie can't answer. All she wants is to get out and move her body, lest her father beat her for
staying out too long.
She looks around to make sense of her situation. "Wait. Why is there a typewriter-looking thing
that's not a typewriter? And what's with the nurse's uniform?" Lottie panics.
"She looks like she can't breathe," someone comments.
"Discharge her so she can go home and rest," the old woman says, removing her warm hand,
which was providing this restless soul with a sense of familiarity.
Charlotte. Lottie, as she is called by many. This woman runs outside in confusion, wondering
where the heck her family is.
Wait, what? There's a yellow-looking car driven by… a woman?
She almost loses consciousness again.
Where am I? What is this place? Is that a girl studying inside a restaurant-looking place? Why is
a lady walking outside without her husband?
No. The world looks changed. There's something unfamiliar. No. EVERYTHING'S unfamiliar.
The horse carriages around the street are gone. There is no street. It's all cement and road.
Lottie starts hyperventilating. She grabs a police officer's hand and pulls.
Looking annoyed, the officer asks, "May I help you?"
Breathing out of relief, she replies, "Could you please contact Mr. Bannerman in North
Tarrytown?"
The officer looks like he's being pranked. "Do you mean Sleepy Hollow? That name changed
about 19 years ago."
Lottie is more confused than ever. She vaguely remembers going there just three months after
her marriage. Clearly, the person is mistaken.
Before she can ask again, the officer leaves.
What is going on? Why are there so many cars outside? What's with the language? And WHAT
IN THE BOONDOGGLE IS THAT GIRL WEARING?
No time for thoughts as her stomach growls. A lady must not let others hear sounds of
embarrassment. This has Lottie running to a building that seems to have a photo of fried fish
outside.
Oh my! Why is there so much light and so many things?
"Could I have some bread with fish stew, please?" she asks politely as she takes in the
atmosphere.
The person in front looks at her strangely but doesn't say anything.
"Of course, ma'am," he finally replies. "Cash or credit?"
Realization hits her. She doesn't have any money!
I don't wanna suffer from hunger like before.
But wait. What was that C word? Red… credit? None of this made any sense to this lost woman
The man says with a look of annoyance, "If you wanna pay through cash, please give me your
ID."
Lottie looks surprised, hearing such an unfamiliar word. "What's that?"
The man looks mad now. "You know, that rectangle-shaped card with your photo and your
birthdate, or do I have to teach you how to read?"
My birthdate? The July of 1930, when my older brother died right after I was born?
The date. Yes, that's what she needs right now. "What's the date?" she asks while
contemplating whether to run or not.
"Look, ma'am, I don't have time for this. There's a calendar behind you. Take a look at the menu
and decide how you are going to pay, or I'm gonna have to call security."
Lottie looks back. The calendar says 2015 in bold.
WHAT? Where am I?
She touches the piece of paper on the wall with shaking hands. Her knees are trembling .
And it all finally comes back to her.
Fall of 1850
A younger version of the same woman looks so happy. Getting married in a respectable family
is the best thing that could happen to a girl. Richard Bannerman was a wealthy, well-known and
well spoken merchant.
One probably wishes his hands were gentle as such.
“Why would you interrupt me with your useless facts? You wish to embarrass me?”Richard
snarls.
Lottie takes a few steps back until her back hits the hard wall. “I only wanted to improvise your
speech” .
“That is not a good wife's job”.
Well she stops counting after the third kick and the fourth punch.
A woman was buried two days after. She often wandered around at night. Crazy they say. It's
not like anybody’s gonna question a man regarding his wife's death.
Present
Lottie reels.
What was that?
My husband? Oh he pushed me down the stairs once. The women here probably don't get
beaten like before.
Alas! Only if she knew.
Is this God’s way of repaying me? I tried my best to be good. Everyday. Mama said that's what a
good girl does. But I don't have to listen to mama anymore.
Well it's not like it matters anyway.
Lottie is happy. Lottie is free. Lottie helps others. Lottie is nice. SHE IS FREE.
What do people write in their notebooks? Maybe they write about dreams,
adventures, or even secret crushes. There's nothing abnormal about it, not
at all. However, for some, the notebook is the safekeeper of tears. The
guardian of strange sketches that have no sensible meaning. But only the
pen and paper recognize those patterns. The patterns that somehow
always find a way into the writer's works. And before the writer knows it, the
thought of the next day fills their entire form with elephantine and
unforgiving dread. It's as if another stack of bricks has been placed
squarely on their shoulders. It's routine. As soon as sleep leaves their
bodies and light reflects on their face, they feel it. It's heavier.
Their walk has this distinct slump; their eyes void of sparkle and their face
lacking those lines and dimples that appear with unadulterated, genuine
joy. Everyone assumes they have poor posture. How can they not? No one
except the reflection in the mirror can see those darn bricks. Life is a debt,
living being the act of each day piling on and on while somehow, people
encourage increasing the burden. Because they can't see those bricks.
Those bricks etched with those patterns of hurt and the past that our brains
try to lock away to protect what's left of our human. We can't exactly see
them, they aren't in front of us, but they're never behind us. They take their
place and bear their weight as if it's their right and when it's quiet enough,
they whisper back to us the words that keep us buried where we are. And
they show themselves on filled pages.
What else do we have? Alongside that unbearable heft, we have guilt
mercilessly pulling from both sides. The guilt of ending this seemingly
unending and completely valueless suffering, the selfishness of it all. What
would happen to our parents? our friends? Who will brush my little sister's-
someone's little sister's hair? You must stay. Stay for them, they need you.
But do they really? Won't they move on? No, of course not. How could they
ever? But, you're not sure.
The other side doesn't spare you. How much longer will you allow yourself
to do this? What have
you
done to deserve this? To live as if your death is
in the next step you take? Why can't you free yourself? Just be selfish for
once, have you not given enough? To everyone else, maybe you have. To
yourself, obviously not. How could you ever give enough. You've never let
yourself receive any of what you give.
It's too much. So after you finish writing your new set of goodbyes to your
loved ones, you take a little peek at the set you wrote for them last time.
You sit down on the floor, the cold tile making you flinch. You think back to
that day. How heavy it was, how unbearable it felt. The tears still stain the
page. You go back to the set prior to that one. And all the ones that came
before it. You don't remember writing this many– I don't remember writing
this many. I can't even recognize the object of my pain on the older pages.
I've forgotten the smiles and scents of some recipients of the letters. I
wonder how such a young version of myself could even think of such a
fate. And when I close the notebook, I think of something, something that
stays trapped in the cage I built for it with my own two hands to protect
myself from the disaster it brings.
The future. What about me with slightly longer hair with a couple more
centimeters to my name. It's a bit unfair that she'll never get to look back at
today's writings isn't it? Yes, yes it is. Quite the injustice, if I so myself. So
as I do every other time, I put the notebook back in its little hiding place–
my mom can never find it, it would break her. My shoulders feel less
slumped than usual. And the next day, my friends compliment me on my
slightly improved posture. The weight of yesterday stays with my notebook
in its hiding place, so for now, I can walk a little easier.
Forgotten, abandoned, left to thought.
No name, no claim, no memories to call.
A breath that lasted only so long,
Forgotten by the barer and the life that caused.
Bloom, blossom, symbol of birth and life
Yet the notion couldn't reach the sights of the
unopened eyes.
Where maternal love should be felt and warm,
Leaves only filth, cold and scorn.
Only to be found by bigger hearts, too late still.
The breath is gone, the nimble chests gone numb,
A life had begun but so soon was it gone.
So woe to the ones unborn and woe to those who were,
only to be forgotten in ditches and sewers.
Love could not find you, nor could warmth.
Your last cry not heard and your life not sworn.
Such fickle life. With no recollection at all.
Such pain it might, but none will they bare at all.
Perhaps that's the blessing they get, the first and last In the short run of life.
the blessing of ignorant bliss in the cruise of cruel might.
Musings of Hades
My lady gathers narcissus
A few tucked away in those locks,
Earth under her soles
Her smile so artless.
My lungs filled with cornflower blues
Her small pollen stained hands
Mine stained with her tear brine
A lump of flesh growing in that grain,
Dried are the carcasses of narcissus
Denial of Calabria on her quivering lips,
Echoing hollow voice asphyxiates me
'Imbecile, bleed the red seedy fruit white!'
My lady gathers essences
A few tucked away in those urns,
Embers under her soles
Her smile so listless.
“Never bite the hand that feeds you”- a phrase ingrained into the bones of
our sons and daughters.
Cherish the hand that feeds you because it can starve you. Love your
parents as deeply as you can because that is how they love you. But what
do you do when those same hands, that mix rice and curry ever so gently
on scratched up Thalis to slowly feed you, strike you down until you see
red? Hurl insults at you until you can recognize what you are? To what
extent are children expected to cherish the parents that claim to love them
unconditionally, but leave scars on their hearts and bodies that love so soft
could never cut. Parents do not love unconditionally, it is the children who
do so.
Children are brought into this world with no one for them. Parents have
spouses, their own friends and family, but a child has no one. No one
except those who brought them here. So the child loves their family,
through all. Justification of pain through the confessions of love keeps them
trapped. Trapped in the belief that their parents love them as deeply as
they do. And so it must be said any kind of abuse to a child is unforgivable.
Let me put it this way, how cruel must you be to push someone who has
nothing to fall back on except for your arms? You cannot push them and
catch them at the same time. Helping them get up won't change the fact
they're already hurt. So why do that exact same thing to children? When
they are hit, yelled at and belittled what can they fall back on? They have
nothing in the world except those who ruin them. It is akin to disarming the
bystanders that have no weapon to begin with.
And these unfortunate children, who can they go to? They're your parents,
they get angry sometimes. They do this because they care about you. Why
are you acting this way? All parents do this. They brought you into this
world, be grateful.
But why is being brought into this world treated as the ultimate debt? The
pain of bearing a child is incomparable, yes, however that does not give
anyone the right to inflict the same or worse pain on the child. How can we
expect someone to pay off a debt they never even signed for, a debt that
doesn't even belong to them? After that, they must be grateful that their
parents fed them and clothed them, as if that's not the basic responsibilities
of a parental figure. Failing to meet those is an inability on the parents' part,
it does not make anyone else better for doing what they can't. So once
again, children are indebted to their parents for things that they have a right
to. A debt that they must pay off with unconditional love.
Who will tell the children that their existence has so much more than an
eternal, boundless debt, more than hurt and loneliness? Who will tell them
their pain is not unjustified, their tears are not more reason to be hurt? No
one. Because children only have their parents. Through those blurry and
tear filled eyes, they beg for forgiveness, for love. They promise to be
better children, to be deserving of love. Because love is earned in the case
of these precious souls, but their love remains unending. And it seems their
parents love them too, until the next time the dam breaks.
No one will try to help, those are familial affairs. Who cares about how a
child is treated, they'll forget it anyway. But these are not matters to forget.
That child will never forget. Each humiliating insult, each unwarranted
critique stamps permanently on to the young impressionable mind. Stamps
they will carry as souvenirs until they muster the courage to stick them onto
a blank letter and send it off. But to the parents, that was just another
Tuesday, they cannot even recall what happened. In fact, did it even
happen at all? These children obviously lie for attention, what an
impressive act.
And after the end credits roll, when the children can no longer withstand it
and leave behind the place and the people that made them want to smash
the mirror to pieces, rip out resemblance of those who brought them into
this world, they're criticized for abandoning their parents. It's as if their
parents didn't abandon them first. Parents are pitied for being in such a
tough position, nobody questions why their own flesh and blood would do
this. Because they'll have to face a reality they can't accept, they
themselves did something wrong, and the children had nothing more to
give. Or, the children will stay. They'll absorb everything that happened to
them and make it their normal. Why? Because not everyone can deal with
the grief of realizing their own parents do not love them. So they decide it's
completely fine. They'll do the same to their own children and bark about
how much worse they had it. It doesn't matter if their kid is in pain at their
hands, they suffered more pain from their own roots. Because these
unloving parents were unloved children too. How could they have ever
known they deserved better? They didn't. So they believe they got exactly
what they deserved, and passed on the same worthlessness to their
children.
It's not to say such parents don't love their children. They do. Technically
they do. But not enough to let go of their ego. Not enough to let go of what
they believe is right, to listen to their child's pleas and feel remorse, to feel
the need to change or apologize. Not enough to face their own pasts and
question why they do what they do. They'll throw a half-hearted apology
alongside a Thali full of cut up fruit and expect wholehearted forgiveness.
However, fruit juice cannot wipe stained cheeks. The sweetness of the fruit
cannot replicate a loving embrace.
It is so easy to love a child. How incredibly beautiful it is watching them
flourish as the person they were meant to be because of that love. So tell
me, can you blame me for resenting those who lock their love behind
achievements, traits, and impossible expectations? All you must do, is love
your child, and reach out your hands to give them all that you can, they
already love you as much as they possibly can.
Can I ask a question?
I presume you'd answer
But do I seek an answer?
I seek the comfort of not knowing.
I seek the blanket of lies you would tuck me under,
It would keep me warm,
So warm,
I would suffocate
My suffering will feel sweet,
The tears I hide may seem a fair receipt,
While the question cuts deeper in my throat
Perhaps I knew the answer all along,
Wouldn't questioning a fraud make my love false?
Would you surrender the lie,
Or make me believe anew?
Maybe I would ask the question
If I knew,
If I Knew
You'd keep me close to you.
No promises
The dining table, the quiet ritual
Elusive words dripping down to your chin
Lips smeared in grease,
Nebulous sighs, saliva in chardonnay
Dark abyss, your dilated pupil
Tar like affection rolling on your tongue
Loose locks gently lulling to rhythm
Thrumming fingers, soup long forgotten.
"It's time" you say,
Leaving behind yet another night,
Smell of cigarettes static in the air.
The man was lying dead in the field. I go ahead and stand very still near him. I looked closely if his chest is moving up and down. Nada.
Scared, I nudge his dress shoes with my feet. No response. My pulse quickens. I slowly move toward him and lean down to check his pulse on his
check. He is irrevocably dead. The few seconds my fingers was in contact with his skin, it was ice cold.
I look down once again with a sharp exhale, my hands shaking.
What do I do now?
This is in the middle of nowhere. There's no one I can call for help.
Do I just leave him behind? Maybe tell someone once I reach the village?
He is wearing a long brown overcoat, the coat is slightly dirty where it is touching the ground. His hair is matted to his forehead, probably from sweat.
Did he run here?
I look around, the tall grasses bending in the wind ever so slightly. There's no sign of struggle. No destroyed grass, no trampled ground. A natural death
perhaps. I turn around, getting ready to leave. I walk off. Or so I thought.
I didn't leave.
The night falls, I am sitting down besides the man's body since then. The man sits up and stares at me. I don't look despite feeling his gaze on me.
He parts his lips saying something unintelligible, as time goes by it becomes clear.
You are lonelier than my corpse.
You finally look at the man. He has no apparent expression on his face, tone dry as he repeats the same line. After a while, he stops and stares at me. I
turn my face away from him.
Who was I going to tell about his death anyways? My loneliness has consumed everything around me. I have nothing.
I stand up, brushing off dirt and grass from sitting down and walk away from there. The sun has risen. The fog beads on the grasses are shining. Isn't
this scene supposed to make me grateful for being alive?
I turn around one more time. He is lying down. He is dead.
The snakes, where should be my hair,
Tremble when they think of Poseidon’s stare
Crumble when they relay the memories in my head
Weep when they unleash Death
The snakes, where should be my hair,
Weep, for they are in a monster’s lair
The lair created by unjust Wisdom
The lair created by the flawed system
Where they fail to provide me vengeance–
Instead, they ask for my repentance.
They pray for my allegiance
But do not right what was wronged.
“Because as a woman to men you belong
Because to be born a woman is to be indebted to men
So you must pay the price every now and then.”
You promote books with a rapist for a male lead–
A trend for thirteen year old schoolgirls with pigtails you feed
Such content written
by women
that taints their imaginations
Until it is desensitized and normalised as sexual temptations.
You push forward posts labelling it “dark romance”
Saying it’s just “fiction” for your gain, for finance,
But hide the posts of screaming women,
Sobbing for their children, raped and killed by powerful men.
Monetise on oh–so romantic–books of dark fictions
Ignore what goes on right in front of us within our nations–
For we are tired of watching videos of the world in rubbles;
We would rather live in rose-tinted bubbles.
With such content, you strip us of our moralities,
Romanticising unpreventable-by-the-law brutalities;
So the little girls grow up and stop caring about people’s pain
For they are busy being turned on by a man’s free rein.

Freedom is a word spoken so often, yet so rarely felt. Of all the forms freedom could take, perhaps flying is the most beautiful—but only for birds. We envy the endless sky they call home, yet are they born knowing how to fly, or
do they fall before they learn to soar?

A bird with black feathers and a heart far too large for its tiny body, lived in a small forest and spent its days among trees, flowers, and butterflies together with its friends. In the quiet forest, storms come here and there, creating a lot of mess in its middle-class nest. The first storm came and took away the little bird's one and only toy. It stopped mourning its toy because of the company of its friends. But soon, it was thrown into a bottomless wall. The sound of its crying echoed inside the empty wall, but no one heard. It tried to flap its dark wings as hard as it could, taking one step closer to the surface only to be pulled three steps deeper inside. It took a long time for Hope to reach the surface, only to see that they were doing great.

Hope fell into darkness more than once. It climbed out each time with trembling wings, only to discover that the world above had continued without it. So Hope flew harder, learned faster, and carried its wounds beneath its feathers where no one ever thought to look beneath.

Every night, while the forest slept, Hope spoke to the lonely moon as though the sky were the only place willing to listen. And every dawn, before the first ray of sunlight touched the leaves, it would lift its wings toward a distant mountain that no other bird believed could ever be reached.

Almost—just almost—before Hope took off toward its dream, another sudden storm came, stole something far greater and took away its dearest. Its dearest vanished with the storm without a sound, making all Hope’s efforts in vain. Agony should have been the first thing to feel, but Hope chose to laugh.
Some losses make us cry.
Others leave us smiling, because tears are no longer enough.

Hope learned that long before it understood the meaning. For no reason, it trapped itself inside its nest and looked at the sky, the clouds, and the other birds every day while singing happily. Staring at the blue sky, Hope didn't realize when its favorite color became green.

Beyond the forest lay an endless field. At its farthest edge stood a mountain dressed in evergreen. Flowers bloomed upon its slopes through every season, and butterflies drifted through the wind as though the mountain itself were breathing. From Hope's nest, it looked impossibly far away, yet impossibility had never frightened it.

Every morning before the sun rose, Hope took flight. Across the endless field it flew, chasing the same distant peak. But there was one cruel rule to the journey; every time it rested, it had to begin again from the nest. Day after day, season after season, those tiny wings carried a dream far larger than themselves.
Then another storm came.
Hope sped up to avoid the rain. Little did it know that, in a storm, rain is not the frightening part—thunder is.
The sky spun.
The mountain vanished.
Feathers scattered into the wind.
Then—
Silence.
The frozen ground reached Hope long before it was ready.

The snow did not burn Hope. It swallowed the sound of the fall, as though the world wished to forget that it had ever fallen at all. White slowly surrendered to crimson, yet the pain did not come from the wound. It came from the silence.
Hope struggled to lift its wings, only to discover there were no feathers left to carry upon the sky.
Night settled over the field. Then came the sound of slow, measured footsteps from all the directions.
"What happened, my little bird?" A deep voice echoed through the empty field. "I thought you almost reached the top of the mountain, sweetie." The voice was deep, calm, and strangely gentle.
Fear may control the body, but curiosity can defeat it in a single blow.
Hope peeked toward the voice, a lone wolf approached through the snow, walking with a limp. With every step, a dark red trail stained the white beneath its paws.
"You are wounded," Hope said for the first time, leaving every other question unasked. “Oh, you noticed,” The wolf laughed softly. Hope nodded, forgetting the fear..
"So are you, sweetie."
It sat beside Hope as though they had known each other for years.
"How did you fall, sweetie?"
"I didn't notice the thunder."
"No wonder they call you a fool." The wolf chuckled.
Hope lowered its eyes.
"A fool?"
"Yes, sweetie. They call you that because you carry what they have long forgotten."
Hope remained silent.
The wolf smiled.
"Hope. Dreams. Courage."
After a long pause, Hope asked quietly,
"Did you once have them too?"
The wolf's laughter faded into the silent night.
"Yes, sweetie."
Its eyes wandered toward the moon.
"I simply failed to notice the trap. (A pause) Do you not love your nest, sweetie?" the wolf asked.
Hope looked toward the moon hanging above the sleeping forest.

"I do," it answered softly. "The forest is calm. It is warm. It has always been my home. But promises and dreams never allowed me to stay. Distant miles kept calling my name, teaching me to fly, to run, and to keep going, even when every part of me longed to hold on."
The wolf listened without interrupting.
"So... you are like me?" Hope asked.
The wolf smiled.

"The pack I belonged to never saw my worth. They believed every wolf must hunt. I never chased prey—I chased fear away. Every claw of fear hated me like I was a plague. That was enough for them to call me useless."
Hope tilted its head.
"Why didn't you live as your nature intended? Aren’t your claws one of those fears?"
"My nature?" The wolf chuckled. "Who decided that being born a wolf meant I had to hunt? Must I become what others expect simply because they named me before they knew me, sweetie?"
After a small pause...
"We are just... us. Living for what we choose to live for."
For the first time that night, Hope smiled.
"You are different."
"We are different," the wolf corrected gently. "We are simply ourselves."
The wind passed between them without a sound.

Night slowly surrendered to dawn. The moon faded beyond the mountains, spring knocked gently upon the world, and the pain of countless struggles sank deep into their bones, just as the melting snow disappeared into the grass. At the same time, they looked at their fading scars not as strangers, but as two souls who had survived the same loneliness in different forms.
As the first light of morning reached the field, Hope whispered,
"Who are we, if we cannot simply be ourselves?"
The wolf raised its eyes to the rising sun.
“ Who will we become when all these scars fade beneath the morning light?"
As uncertainty met the rising sun, would Resurgam become the beginning of their own stories?
Perfect
Syeda Nafisa Tarannum
Sheren looked around her picturesque, humble abode. Despite the modest setting of the
not-so-spacious apartment, she ensured that all was prim and proper, everything placed where
they were supposed to be, resulting in a vision that could easily be a cover for the coming week’s
issue of
Architectural Digest
. Every single thing looked perfect, just the way her husband had
taught her. Twenty years of marriage with Urshif had conditioned Sheren to believe everything
had to be immaculate, there was no excuse for imperfection. She felt a tinge of pride imagining
how the people she expected later would walk through the apartment, and fail to hide their
admiration for all its spick-and-span nooks and crannies.
She fluffed up the already “plushy to the core of every microfibre” cushions, slid her dainty
fingers across the tabletop she had spent hours scrubbing until it reflected the light gleaming
above, admired her recently acquired mirrors, only to pause before the heavy metal frame she
had been meaning to avoid. Still crooked. Still not sitting right. It enclosed a beautiful still from
their wedding night - Urshif seated on a high chair, looking deviously handsome, with Sheren
standing behind him still resembling the teenager she had been just two years prior to that night.
Perhaps she could try one more time to budge the frame into symmetry before people arrived,
but she had been unsuccessful before and doubted she had any strength left in her to attempt it
again. She stared at the rare sign of distortion in her house- the askew frame- for a minute or two,
sighed and moved on.
As she walked across her pantry, she flinched at the sight of her freezer, which had been
struggling since the day before yesterday, had now completely failed her. It was now emanating
the kind of smell that no amount of lemons, vinegar or baking soda could get rid of. Pinching her
nose and she walked towards the freezer, and was content upon ensuring that, functional or not,
at least the freezer looked spotless on the outside. “Good”, she thought to herself, she was sure
that certain things would eventually lead people to this freezer and she had to make sure they
would admire how neat it looked from the outside. Almost as if it had been bought just
yesterday.
Urshif believed that no paid help would ever care for the house as if it were their own. He trusted
only Sheren to be capable of keeping the house spotless. She took upon the job with fierce
intensity, going over every sweep, every brush, every scrub twice. Urshif needed her to be on top
of things, she had been after all entrusted with the responsibilities of keeping everything- perfect.
The wobbly stool in the corner of the room caught her eye. The same stool which had once
escaped her sight , allowing the dust resting on it evade her duster. Urshif had walked into the
room and noticed the unclean surface while trying to grab something from the shelf beside it. Six
legs suffered that day. Five endured the pain, but the sixth leg—one of the legs on the
four-legged stool—bore the brunt of his wrath and broke. Urshif decided to not discard it, as
keeping it around would serve as a reminder to Sheren. She would never ever be negligent again.
Sheren had only ever cooked rice when she was living with her parents. Urshif was disgruntled
when he learnt that she did not know how to prepare half the dishes he had been listing down for
his wife to concoct at his command. Her mother once detected the strain in her voice over the
phone one night after dinner, and through call after call, she had mentored Sheren until she
turned into the most skillful cook her son-in-law claimed he deserved. Not that this prevented the
occasional outbursts, which may or may not have resulted in a scar across her right shoulder after
a hot bowl of curry was thrown at her. Nor did her precision in measuring the spices or
elaborating the cooking techniques spared her from scornful criticisms in the presence of guests.
Today, after what felt like years, she was taking a break from cooking, as for the first time since
she had started living here, she would not have to entertain the people coming over.
Throughout the initial years of their conjugal life, Sheren tried her utmost to please her husband
who seemed unimpressed by everything she embodied. Urshif made certain that she knew he had
married below him, having compromised when it came to her looks and complexion, solely
because he wanted a “simple” wife. He was downright disappointed by the fact that Sheren’s
father, who should have been on cloud nine at having successfully snagged a true gentleman for
his daughter, had not offered him certain “gifts and presents” that any other parent would have
given out of elation.
The years that followed were laced with painful miscarriages, which were, of course, perceived
as failure on Sheren’s part. Urshif the kind and generous, upon learning after her fifth
miscarriage that she can never conceive again, did not choose to leave her and remarry. Why she
was not always worshipping the ground he walked upon baffled him, for she had failed him
while he had given her a life, which warranted a level of gratitude she could only repay by
serving him eternally.
Twenty years in, Sheren had been moulded into a mute, numb entity. Just the way it should be in
Urshif’s world. However, she had shown a sign of inefficiency- she could not fix the lopsided
frame. It required some hammering, an expertise she had unfortunately failed to establish in her
two decades of training. He begrudgingly took on the task, but the problem, apparently, was
neither in the frame’s structure, nor the placement of the hook, or skills of the expert holding the
hammer. It was her father’s. The same father whose death anniversary was just the day before,
whose voice had been ringing in her ears for weeks leading up to the anniversary, whose
memories had been burning her insides all over again as the date approached. The father who
had not been a generous father-in-law. Had the apartment he had invested his life’s savings in
been given to Urshif, all would have been well and such a disastrous inconvenience would never
have befallen him.
Not realising that words were escaping her mouth, she had uttered a begging for not bringing her
father into the matter. Thanks to sheer luck, the hammer that flew towards her narrowly brushed
past her left ear. Urshif then stomped across the room to sit in front of the television, because his
mood had been ruined and now he needed to relax and regain composure.
Sheren stood still for a long time. Urshif, displeased as usual, did not look at her or care to see
where the hammer had landed. The television continued to play. Then, with abnormal calmness,
she grabbed the hammer with her unusually steady hand and struck the back of Urshif’s head.
Thrice. Urshif’s heart that she had clogged with calories over the years by serving him endless
successions of delicious treats, finally returned the favour and gave up without much of a fight.
Chopping him up and fitting his body parts into the freezer did not take much effort, as she had
spent years organising months’ worth of meat supplies in that very storage space. It took two full
days of relentless hard work to clean up all the mess. But the smell had been growing
increasingly intense as the freezer struggled to contain her secret. It had now wafted out of the
apartment and would soon attract the rightful attention of her neighbours. People would soon be
here - people in the neighbourhood who smelled something fishy, people who had noticed
Urshif’s absence, the police, the journalists. Everyone would come and see what a perfectly
beautiful home Sheren had maintained over all these years. Everything neatly sorted, cautiously
organised, carefully maintained. Even her beloved husband’s body, cleaned and packed with
delicate dexterity. Just the way Urshif had taught her, every single thing was just- perfect.

The Architecture of an Unwitnessed Life
There are people who enter our lives so quietly that we cannot identify the precise moment
they begin to haunt us. They do not arrive like disasters. They arrive ordinarily: through
hallways, passing conversations, fleeting glances — the accidental intersection of two
otherwise unremarkable lives.
Then, for reasons we cannot adequately defend, they become extraordinary.
Not necessarily because they possess anything extraordinary, but because we begin to place
extraordinary things upon them. Their silence becomes a language. Their smallest gestures
begin carrying disproportionate weight, and in someone’s memory, it is etched as a
philosophy of hope.
The tragedy is that the other person may never know. They continue living their life. They
forget conversations another person has replayed for years.
Two people can inhabit the same memory without ever having shared the same experience.
We tend to believe suffering requires an event like a rejection, a betrayal or a goodbye.
However, some of the most enduring forms of pain arise from what never really happened.
There is no relationship to mourn, no promise to break, no definitive ending to make the grief
comprehensible.
How does one grieve an
almost
Or was it even an almost from the other end?
So, the mind, intolerant of unfinished things, begins constructing its own explanations. It
takes fragments and builds architecture from them. A glance becomes a window. A silent
ritual with them becomes the foundation stone. Eventually, the architecture becomes more
convincing than the ground upon which it stands.
And the person who built it begins to live inside.
However, something else happens, too. You become aware that someone is watching.
Before someone else's opinion matters to us, we are relatively free. We can be awkward,
ridiculous, excessive, ordinary. We can experiment with different versions of ourselves
without wondering which one will survive in someone else's memory.
Then the self acquires an audience.
Every action develops a possible interpretation. Every mistake feels permanent. Every
embarrassing moment becomes something that might have been witnessed and remembered.
We begin to see ourselves from the outside, through a pair of eyes whose judgment we cannot
control.
One no longer wishes simply to be liked.
One wishes to be correctly understood.
One wishes for the humiliating chapters to be contextualised. To have the strange behaviour
explained. To have the worst version of oneself recognised as an aberration rather than a
revelation.
You saw me, but you did not see all of me.
So, the performance begins.
One becomes more careful about the construction of a life that might look interesting from a
distance. One hopes that they will one day be understood for their behaviour based on how
much they have changed now. There is nothing inherently false about it, but the cruelty
begins when they must eventually be witnessed by the person whose gaze we have
internalised before they can feel real.
A life becomes a portfolio submitted to an absent examiner. Yet, the examiner never asked for
it.
We begin asking questions that appear to concern another person but are, in truth, questions
about ourselves.
What will they remember?
Have I changed enough?
What would they think of my present self?
Beneath these questions lies another: is it possible to become someone new without first
being forgiven for who we used to be?
Perhaps this is why certain people become so difficult to forget. They become attached not
merely to our desire for them, but to our desire to revise ourselves.
We mistake the two longings for one.
We believe we want their attention, when what we may want is an opportunity to stand before
them without shame. We believe we want them to choose us, when what we may want is
proof that the person we once were is no longer the only person we can be.
The distinction is difficult to perceive because both desires occupy the same body. Both can
make an ordinary day feel unbearable. Both can turn a passing notification into an event of
unreasonable magnitude.
This is why another person's happiness can hurt in ways that seem disproportionate to the
event itself. A glimpse of a life continuing without us.
However, another person's happiness is not an accusation. Perhaps freedom begins when we
can encounter a reminder without turning it into a measure of our worth. When we can wear
something because we like it, listen to a song because it belongs to us, and allow these things
to exist without the tormenting thought of how they might appear through another person's
eyes. Their judgement is not a verdict on our own worth.
We may never discover what someone from our past thinks of us. We may never know
whether they remember us fondly, despise our existence, or rarely think of us at all. We may
never receive the conversation that would place everything in its proper proportions.
However, we must accept:
they do not owe us an ending.
This is not a satisfying conclusion. It offers no final correction of the past. It asks something
harder of us — that our lives remain livable even when certain questions remain unanswered.
Perhaps maturity is not the moment we finally receive the explanation we wanted. Perhaps it
is the moment we realise that even if the explanation came, it could not return the years we
spent waiting for it.
I sometimes think of the self as a house.
We spend our early years building rooms without knowing what they are for. Some are bright
and open. Others are constructed hurriedly around our fears. We leave certain doors
unlocked, hoping someone will enter and understand what we have made.
When they do not, we begin decorating the rooms they never saw.
We imagine their eventual return.
We keep the lights on.
Years pass. The house changes. New rooms appear. Old walls are repainted. We discover
windows opening onto landscapes we could never have anticipated. We meet people who sit
with us without requiring us to explain every room.
And still, sometimes, we find ourselves listening for footsteps at the front door.
Not necessarily because we want the person outside, but because we have spent so long
believing that their arrival would prove the house was worth building.
One day, perhaps, we notice the absurdity of it. We have missed entire evenings of our own
life listening for someone who may not even know the address.
So we turn off the porch light.
Not in anger. Not to punish the person who never arrived.
We turn it off because there are things to do inside.
The house was never supposed to be a monument to an absent guest.
It was supposed to be a place to live.
So, perhaps that is the quietest form of freedom was not becoming someone worth
witnessing, but realising that you were never required to be witnessed at all.
THE DAWN
The Rosewood town is well known for its high peace index. People call it the City of Serenity.
No chaos, no fight, no hurdles, just people living their everyday life. All thanks to the collective
efforts of the town people and the town government.
One night near the 16th street residential area a girl was walking. Her clothes were disheveled
and torn, her body was badly bruised in multiple places, red blood soaking her clothes and a
broken arm. She was walking almost like a sleepwalker. The outside injury was visible but her
inside was screaming yet she remained silent. People tend to forget emotions when it may be too
heavy to even bear. She passed out.
The upcoming days passed in a daze. Police came , media came and the matter was dragged to
court. Today is the final hearing. The handcuffed criminal was presented before the judge. The
criminal kept head down but could feel the people watching.
Soon the hearing started. The Judge said:
- The violent and brazen behaviour of the culprit is a threat to the town’s long perceived
reputation. The court has decided to place the culprit in The Justice Cell for breaking the
town codes of peace.
The culprit finally looked at the judge. Her face is still swollen. She asked:
- What is my fault, my lord? They are the ones who ruined me. They are the ones who
permanently damaged my right arm . I can’t even lift a kettle.
- Your suffering is valid but Rosewood values peace over everything and your active
decision to choose a rather unsafe area is something the court cannot overlook.
Rose looked at her father in the back. His back crooked with shame. She goes silent.
- The court is adjourned for today.
The judge declared. Rose is dragged in a chain. Tons of people and the media shaming her. They
put her in a car and drive away. She stares at those camera flashes and those judging faces. She
doesn’t see faces, only masks.
They arrive at the Justice Cell. It is a barren area covered with 50ft grey walls around it. Beside it
there is a massive field. Grass trimmed, walls painted, the field stands in a contrast to the grey,
lifeless cell building. In the centre of the field there is a stage or a hanging podium.
They hand her over to the jailor. The jailor shows her the cell room she is assigned. A cramped
two bed room with a basin and an unknown smell. She sees a girl staring at her. The jailor
introduces her to Lara, her jailmate. Jailor asks Lara to show Rose the place and tell her all the
rules and regulations.
Lara finally moved and came closer. Then she asked Rose to follow her. They started walking.
Lara suddenly broke the silence and said:
- You were assaulted? Your family must be in trouble. They outcast people like these.
- I know but here you are equal. No one questions anything here. After today you are not
allowed to ask anything to anyone about the outside.
- Ah.. Fine.
- Breakfast starts at sharp 8. If you come late you go hungry. Then at 9 starts chores. The
warden will explain your duties. You will find your clothes at the laundry and you can't
wear anything besides the jail clothes. Do you understand?
Rose nodded. They walk through an eerie dark hallway with a bunch of cell rooms. Some
opened, some closed. Rose suddenly notices a room with an open door. A man sits alone in the
dark room with a doll in his hand. A little penguin.
- His neighbour killed his daughter. He put the man's house on fire. He was arrested for
arson. After all, who leaves a 5 year old alone at home?
Lara keeps moving. Rose stays. She did wrong. She brought shame to her family. The whole
society blames and berates her. Everyone here is the culprit. Then why something feels wrong.
She asks:
- Lara? May I know your story?
- I said. No question about life outside.
- How long is it here?
- You stay until those wounds feel numb. Then you sign a waiver and be free.
- Waiver?
- It means you admit your mistake and the society takes you back in.
- What if….. I don't?
- Then…..
Lara suddenly stops in her place and looks back. She says:
- Then the Dawn comes for you.
Something in her expression stopped Rose from questioning further.
The night falls. Rose sits by the wall. Her eyes hollow. She closes her eyes. When she opens
them again she finds herself in an unknown room. The roof is moldy, cracked and leaking. Floor
cold as ice. The walls are covered with big mirrors like a maze. She panics. While calling for
help, she discovers her mouth is sewn shut with thick threads. She stands, struggling to get a
word out. Only muffled sounds. She sprints across the room. She feels like roaches are crawling
up from her throat to get out. She tries tearing the stitches with hand. But in vain. She sees her
reflection in the mirror. Her bruised face filled with tears, snorts and blood. How pathetic she
looks. She can't look at it. But the room is covered with mirrors. How can she escape her own
reflection? She knows how. Shreds of glass are scattered across the room. Her hands are a bloody
mess. Does Rose think breaking the mirror also wipes away the image?
Rose wakes up panting. She fell asleep. She doesn’t see Lara anywhere, just a note saying :
I was his daughter also. My mother never knew he was married before. I just wanted to take my
rights back. But I became a convicted criminal for harassment and defamation. I didn't fight.
Because you can't win against someone who accepts silence as the only form of peace.”
~ Lara
Rose read this, folded it carefully before placing it on the bed. She goes out. In the entrance
hallway she sees a large line of people. Face covered. Like herds moving in the same direction.
Towards the empty field with the hanging stage. She also notices the Penguin doll clutched by a
man in the row. She whispers to herself:
- Their Dawn has finally come.
She hurries to the dining hall. She can't go hungry. She takes food and sits on a bench to eat. Her
shoulder tilted in a specific direction. Her exhaustion is visible in her position. But she slowly
merges to the crowd in a grey painting.
EID
Once the village Molla said , “ Eid is the largest festival of Muslims. It is equally blissful and
pleasant for everyone”. Raju was there too. He listened. He thought to himself was eid really a
joyful experience for all?
Today is the day of Eid. Raju was sleeping under a bridge. There was no hurry in his actions.
He starts observing. The people, their new clothes, joyous faces. Raju doesn’t have those. His
worn out pants, oversized torn shirt, rough and flaky skin, rustic hair make him seem like a
withered flower in a pool of fresh roses . He stands and starts walking. Underneath his calm
face his mind was bustling. The memories of the past were flashing before his eyes creating an
unnatural sense of numbness.
Raju once had a home. A small, quiet home near the Meghna. His father was a boatman. He
remembers how he used to spend hours on the boat. The waves violently shook the boat. The
figure of his father standing tall at the edge of the boat against those waves. It has been ages
since he felt that secure and protected. He recalls his mother running behind him across the shore
with food to feed him. Her long dark hair waved by the wind. He also had a sister. He tries to
remember her face everyday but the vision stays blurred. He just remembers a hand clutching his
hand and running after they stole mangoes from their neighbour’s tree. A hand gently putting a
soaked cloth on his forehead when he had fever.
3 years ago Meghna took his home along with his sister and father in river erosion. His mother,
a new widow, driven from the loss of her husband and daughter decided to leave the village
forever. Just like that Raju came to Dhaka with his mother on a train, without a ticket. Perhaps
this was a reason the city never accepted them. Within 6 months his mother died from Cholera
leaving a 7 year old Raju to fetch alone.
Today Raju has decided to walk through the city and see how the city built on cement and rust
celebrates eid where thousands of dreams are buried under rubbles of reality. He notices a
family of four. Just like his own family. They are dressed nicely and are busy celebrating. Raju
tries to smile like them but his reflection on the roadside glass wall doesn't seem polished
enough . He stops staring and continues walking.
Raju’s family was poor. They didn’t get new clothes or elaborate dinners but Eid was peaceful.
His joy was a simple boat ride or visiting a village fair on his father’s shoulder. Why did fate
have to snatch something so simple from him? In his imagination Meghna isn’t a river, it is a
vile, unsightly demon that took everything from him.
What time is it , maybe afternoon who knows? Raju rests near a field. It is packed with people.
Some chatting, some laughing. Raju spots a dog amid the crowd. Hunger and thirst clear in its
eyes. No one notices it, just like Raju.
Today Raju finally found the answer. Eid isn’t for everyone.
The questions remain silent. Raju continues to walk.
When you look into my eyes,
what is it that you see?
The carefree girl you once hoped to be,
or a stranger wearing the face of your dreams?
When your thunder spills through the walls,
I search myself for the fault,
as though guilt were a language
my blood had learned before my tongue.
Mother, could I have been a better child,
or was I simply born with too many edges
for the shape you wished to give me?
I was four when you pulled me by the hair
and taught the doorway the shape of my leaving,
four when my favourite doll fell from the window.
I watched it descend, a little piece of me
learning how easily I had to let go —
of the things that meant the world to me.
I was six when the wooden sticks bloomed bruises
across the small country of my skin,
and now I wonder if every friendship I bury
is another offering laid at your feet.
You did not like the company I kept,
and so I learned to leave people
before they could become important.
Look at me now, Mother.
Look at the empty spaces beside me—
you created a wreckage in the name of a perfect daughter.
You call it love, this thorned vine around my throat,
this garden in which even my breathing must grow
according to the direction of your light.
You want me first, above every name—
crowned with a future bright enough to blind us both.
But what if my heart dreams of smaller things?
A little house, sunlight gathering quietly upon the floor,
a life that does not need to conquer the world
to justify its existence.
You say you would be happy with that.
Yet your expectations keep growing teeth.
Tell me, Mother, when did your protection
begin to resemble a cage,
and when did I learn to call its bars devotion?
I have stood at this crossroads so long
that Janus has carved two faces into my heart,
one turned towards you, one towards the door.
When I walk towards myself, your tears follow me;
when I turn back, I feel my own soul
clawing at the walls of its confinement.
What am I to do with a love
that makes leaving feel like murder
and staying feel like a slow disappearance?
You, who made your dreams out of my bones,
who buried your own name beneath the weight of mine.
You, who has sacrificed her whole life
to give me mine.
Sometimes I look at you and see something divine,
a woman whose hands could coax flowers from stone,
and I wonder if I am cruel
for remembering the thorns beneath the roses.
I love you, Mother, and I hate the shape of my hurt;
I wish I could separate the two
without tearing myself open.
You once said your sisters had sons
and you had been given a snake.
I was five, but the words took root
somewhere beneath my ribs,
and even now I feel them stirring
whenever I mistake my existence for a burden.
I try to imagine the girl you were,
the expectations that coiled around your youth.
Perhaps you were hurting too,
passing down a language no one taught you to question.
But I was five, Mother,
and I did not know how to translate your wounds
without believing they were my fault.
You tell me you were happy to have me,
and I believe you.
That is the ache I cannot pull from my skin.
How can the same hands cradle and wound?
How can the same heart shelter and suffocate?
I want to understand you without becoming
another place where your sorrow comes to live.
And still, I want to sit beside you.
But I also want to sit as far away as I can.
Your cries from the other room reach for me,
and I am torn between comforting your grief
and wanting to silence the noise of our suffering.
Tell me, Mother, how do I choose myself
when your heartbreak feels etched into my skin?
I cannot keep making a home of my own undoing,
cannot keep offering pieces of my heart
to prove that I am grateful for the life you gave me.
Beneath all this wreckage,
there is still a girl who loves her mother,
and a mother she is still trying to love.
I do not know which of us
I must leave behind to become myself.
I only know that I am tired
of disappearing in the name of love.
Ammu was a ghost.
The most youthful face of my mother that I know, exists only in her old
study. Blue glasses perched upon her nose, red pen in hand, hunched over
reading medical textbooks larger than my head. I would tumble into her
study, crawl onto her lap and bask in her singing. She'd stroke my hair and
play back to me the songs she had already sung to me countless times
while still studying. I would drift off to lands I can imagine no longer and
when I woke up, and it would be time to leave, my Ammu would be gone
again.
Those are the only images of my mother that I can really recall from my
earliest days. Even those memories are a bit unclear after so many years
collecting dust. As becomes a mirror in an abandoned home. However, the
inspiration I felt in those moments; They're as clear and fascinating as a
snow globe seemingly unaffected by time, the fake snow swirling around as
effortlessly as it did so many years ago.
But now that I'm older, even in my hazy memories I see something my
younger self could've never noticed. My young, awestruck eyes could never
catch the guilt in her glossy ones. The guilt of being unable to be with her
baby. The guilt of only being able to give her child time in the dark embrace
of midnight.
How I wish I could go back and hold her hands, her hands worn out with
years of mastering surgical tools, and trace over each dent and
imperfection. I'd tell her that her guilt has sown the seeds of who I am now.
Never once did I feel compelled to blame her for her position. Because
something that I've carried from my childhood, is the inspiration she gives
me. Her absence in the day never felt like neglect. Knowing she was out
there bringing children into the world, while hers were so far away inspired
my love for medicine. Her strength to study till the crack of dawn even after
such tiring days made me want to do the same. The love that cut through
her fatigue, came through her hands that patted my head, keeps me going
even now. The garden of myself has bloomed from my mother's guilt. I wish
I could have shown her this garden before her guilt became a part of her. It
walks alongside her. The garden, however, is all hers. And when it's in
bloom, all of these flowers will be addressed to her.
She's revived from her apparition status nowadays. However, the guilt has
never left her irises. Her shadow seems to slump more than she does.
Whenever she forgets a small detail, or she's late to lunch, I see it. I hear it
in her rushed apologies. No matter how many times I tell her it's okay, I feel
that her guilt enveloped her long ago. It trapped her in the remorse that tells
her she is not an adequate mother. She tells me she has no regrets, but I
can see it in her eyes. The composure grows tired of sticking onto her face
and slips off sometimes. Its fall reveals her shame.
I am my mother's daughter; I inherited her round eyes, her distinct lips, her
silly facial expressions that come out when she's teasing, and the
immovable guilt that haunts her. It flowed into me through her tight hold.
The guilt of being the nothing more than ordinary daughter to an
extraordinary woman. The guilt of not being half of all that she wants me to
be. As her grievances show in her eyes, I believe mine have transfused
into my form. The garden of my person is a product of my mother's endless
guilt. But it could never be her fault. She could've never known her
resentment towards herself would become genetic. And she must not know
now. These thorny flowers are far too dangerous even for her experienced
hands. They can pierce through my skin and draw blood as I hide them
behind my back, I will sweep away the blood that drips down so it may
never reach my daughter. This guilt will end with me, and so I will never
hand these flowers over to her. She can never know the parts that will hurt
her.
And if carrying her share of prickly stems will free her from her pain, I will
tattoo red all over my hands so she must never see the blood drawn from
their thorns.
THE PINK PETALS
For the last thirty years, Rahima had known the world through her window.
Thirty years of marriage, being a wife, a mother, a sister-in-law, a daughter
-in-law, an accountant, a cook, a sweeper. She had been through it all.
Sometimes her husband liked to joke with his friends about how she had
gone through every kind of mundane job for minimum wages.
Thirty years ago, she was a first-class graduate in biology and wanted to
have a job.
So, her parents thought, if she was capable enough to have a job, then she
was capable enough to handle a family. Within a month, before she could
make a scene about it, she was married to a man she barely knew. But she
was a mature girl, said her parents and her relatives; she was capable of
performing her duties as a wife, they said.
Her mother-in-law wanted a daughter-in-law to stay in the house. Her
husband said, “I don’t mind.” Rahima said nothing.
Today’s cycle was also the same. The weekend holiday at their home was
like an open invitation to all. Her husband's friends liked to come and have
lunch.
Faint sounds of their gossip about politics came through the kitchen
doors. When she listened again, her husband made the same joke about
her being capable of doing all kinds of mundane jobs for minimum wages.
Everyone laughed; she tried to laugh.
She again looked through her window. She knew the mango tree’s moods,
the vegetable seller’s call at ten. The exact hour the sunlight crossed the
stove. Her eyes fell on the cherry tree in her neighbour's garden. Its white-
pink petals looked so beautiful that her heart soared with happiness that
she hadn’t felt in a long time.
Her daughter Nisha had said that it looked like cherry blossoms, which are
mostly found in Japan. From then on, Rahima had an affection for cherry
blossoms. She found a photograph of cherry blossoms in Japan, pale pink
against a pale sky. She had cut it out, pressed it inside her old Quran-sharif
cover, and kept it hidden there.
Her husband called her, “Hey, is the lunch ready? Everyone is hungry. Hurry
up”.
“It's almost ready. Give me twenty minutes,” Rahima said.
She had made a spread of about eight dishes. At fifty, she could make fifty
dishes without a recipe, and no one had ever once asked what she wanted
to eat.
Everyone was seated at the table. Rahima began serving the main course
to her husband’s friends.
She called her daughter, Nisha, dear, come down for lunch. “
“Coming, Mama.” Her daughter replied from upstairs.
“Isn’t your daughter already twenty-six? Rafiq,” asked one of her husband’s
friends.
A familiar uneasiness crept over Rahima. She knew what question would
come next. “ Yes, she is. She graduated from her college this year. She is
planning to pursue a master’s degree .”
Rahima answered, feeling proud of her daughter.
As if Rahima sensed it, the question came from her husband's friend.
Because the very next second the friend said, That's good, but isn’t she
getting late? Aren’t you finding a suitable boy for your daughter's
marriage?”
Her husband answered, completely avoiding Rahima’s gaze, “Yes, we are
looking around, but I think it should be my daughter’s choice. Young
people make their own decisions these days. If I find someone suitable
and she likes him, then we can proceed.”
Rahima felt a brief wave of relief. She had expected a different answer
from her husband.
Just then, Nisha came downstairs and took her seat at the table.
“Mama, sit with us,” said Nisha,
“No, dear, I will eat later,” Rahima answered, placing the sweet dish on the
table.
“Hey, you should eat too,” one of her husband’s friends remarked.
“Yes, sit down,” said her husband added, taking a second helping of food.
Rahima was about to sit when he spoke again.
“Hey, where are the pickled chiles? The food doesn’t taste the same
without them .”
“Yes, let me get them.”
Rahima rose from her chair and returned to the kitchen.
Nisha looked at her mom and sighed.
" You know, Dad, pickled chiles give you indigestion; I suggest you stop
eating them, " Nisha said, looking straight into her father's eyes, smiling.
And the lunch went on.
In the evening, when the house slept, Rahima finished cleaning the kitchen
with Nisha tagging along with her.
“Mama, sometimes it’s okay to not get up from the table, you know.
Dad can fetch things, you know.” Nisha said, not looking at her mother as
she scrubbed the pans in soapy water.
Rahima shushed her and said, “Don’t say things like that. I know what’s
going on in your mind, but don’t think about your father like that. He is not
a perfect person, but who is perfect in this world?
“So you know what I think? “ Nisha said, almost dropping the pans.
“Careful with those, dear. “ Rahima said.
”Okey okey…..” Nisha said while hiding her smile.
After finishing their work, both of them sat down on the sofa.
The afternoon had just ended; the alarm clock on the coffee table dinged,
indicating it was afternoon tea time. And her mother-in-law’s time to take
medicine.
“You go and take rest, Nisha,” Rahima said while getting up from the sofa
to give her mother-in-law medicine.
Her mother-in -law was sick these days. So, she liked to make visits to her
friends; she said it makes her feel better.
“Grandma was at her friend's home again, Mama,” asked Nisha.
“Yes, she even had lunch there, after making me cook for her according to
her diet.”
“But she didn’t eat anything; she said she was full,” Nisha said in a
surprised tone while flipping through magazines on the table.
“Yes, dear, these things happen. Don’t get shocked.” Said Rahima while
fixing her headscarf and knocking at her mother-in-law’s door.
“Come in.” Rahima’s mother-in-law said. Nisha watched her mother enter
her grandmother’s room.
Nisha stood up from the sofa when she knocked on the Quran Sharif,
“Ishhh,” Nisha said while picking up the Quran Sharif and noticed a
photograph of Japan’s Mount Fuji with cherry blossom trees covering the
sides of the picture.
Nisha smiled, looking at the photo, and put it back inside the Quran Sharif
A few weeks had passed, and everything was the same, like routine office
work.
“Mama,” said Nisha one night, sitting on the edge of her bed. ” You
remember the university I applied for a scholarship to? I got a reply from
them. I had to go to Japan for the final round of the interview on campus.”
“Alhamdulillah, oh my God, I knew it,” Rahima said, wiping the tears that
had started flowing.
“Let’s go and tell you, Dad " Rahima said, standing up from her bed.
“Mama, listen,” Nisha said while holding her mother’s hands.
“ I already applied for a visa for you and me with the money I saved while
working and the savings account you set up for me “
“Okay, but why me? Did you ask your father?”
“I asked you.” Nisha held out her phone. ”One application for me, and one
for you.”
On the screen was a visa form: Mrs. Rahima Akhter. Her own name, in
capital letters, on something that was hers.
Rahima's hands trembled. Your father will never allow it.”
“I’m not asking him to allow it,” Nisha said gently. “I’m asking you if you
want to go.”
The silence stretched. Somewhere outside, a rickshaw bell rang. Then, in a
voice she barely recognized, Rahima whispered, “ I don’t think it is a good
idea. Your grandmother is sick these days, and your father won’t be able to
handle the household”.
Even as she said it, she was already standing, smoothing her sari, heading
for the door. ”Let me tell your father. He should hear it from me first…”
Nisha caught her wrist lightly. “Mama. Don’t go to him yet.”
Rahima stopped. She looked at her own hand in her daughter’s and then at
the door, as if the old path through it were still the only one she knew.
“Just sit with it for tonight,” Nisha said. That’s all I’m asking.”
Slowly, Rahima sat back down on the edge of the bed.
Next morning,
When the sweet rays of morning sun hit the bedroom curtains, it was
already a few hours since Rahima had woken up. She could not sleep and
kept thinking about what Nisha had said. Fishing out the photograph from
the Quran Sharif, she looked at it. Her heart said, "Go, go for the first time in
her life, do something you would enjoy."
But the second the thought came, she dismissed it. During this time, she
finished her morning prayer and ironed her husband’s clothes for his office.
When she came out of their room,
“Ahhh.. Rahima almost let out a scream because Nisha was standing in
front of their bedroom door, and tea and breakfast were ready on the table.
“Mama, see, I made breakfast. So, what do you think about going to Japan
with me for a few days ?” Nisha said in one breath.
“ Wow.. My daughter finally woke up before 7 A.M.” Dismissing Nisha’s
question, Rahima looked over the table with breakfast her daughter had
made: bread and butter, but fruits cut on a plate.
“Mama, please, you have to think about it. This chance will not come again.”
“You burnt the flatbreads . Now the breakfast is half done. You know your
grandmother won’t eat it.”
“Come on, mama, I saw her eating bread, butter, and jam when you went
out to water the plants. Nisha said, “ Please think about it ”
Rahima looked at her daughter with a smile.
“I will think about it,” Rahima said just to calm her daughter down.
For the rest of the day, Nisha followed her mother from room to room,
returning to the subject whenever she found an opening. Rahima tried to
ignore her, but her daughter’s persistence followed her even into the
quietest corners of the house.
“ Rahima , Rahima…. Where are you?” called her mother-in-law.
“Yes, coming,” Rahima shouted back. It was almost dinner time. Rahima
was setting the dinner table.
“Where are my glasses? Where did you put it ?”
“They are maybe on the side table beside your bed or in the cupboard,
ma,” Rahima answered while coming out of the kitchen.
“They are not there; come fast and find them .”
“They are there, Ma; please look for them,” Rahima said as she was
removing the pot carrying her vegetable stew before it burned down.
“They not there, I am old that you are ignoring me, right?. I wouldn’t have
married my son to you if I knew you would disobey like this. Your parents
hadn’t taught you how to respect your in-laws.” Rahima’s mother-in-law,
Mrs. Akhunessaa, said with a wail that shook their home.
Nisha stomped out of her room and went to her grandmother’s room and
looked for her glasses in her cupboard. After finding them, she gave it on
her grandmother’s hand and without saying anything went out of her room.
“Like mother, like daughter; if the mother doesn’t know how to respect
how, will the daughter learn to respect?” Mrs. Akhunessa murmured under
her breath.
It was a regular thing that happened in this house. 78-year-old Mrs.
Akhunessa made sure that Rahima knew that she didn’t like her daughter-
in-law, even after 30 years of their marriage, the reason Rahima hadn’t
found out. It got even more serious after Nisha’s birth.
Later that night, Rafiq came home from the office and sat down to dinner.
Between mouthfuls, his mother began her list. The rice was too soft. The
vegetables had too much salt. Rahima had talked back. The maid had
been paid too much. Rahima had left the clothes out in the sun too long.
Nisha looked at her father, who kept eating, and at her grandmother, who
was serving her father more rice.
When her grandmother finished and shuffled back to her room, Nisha
asked her father,” Grandmother said bad things to Mama this evening.”
Rafiq said quietly, ”Don’t mind her. She’s getting old. Tell your mother to
ignore it. I’ll talk to her.”
Rahima heard them.
“Yes, I know, Rahima said. “I have been ignoring this for a long time.” Her
voice was firm, maybe the first time in years. Maybe the thread of patience
she had been holding onto was finally close to its breaking point.
Her husband, Rafiq, always said this. He never said anything to his mother,
and sometimes she wished her husband would actually talk to his mother
about this. Maybe this time she had enough.
After dinner, while they cleared the table, Rahima took her daughter's
hands, who was helping her, still wet from the dishes.
“ Let’s go to Japan, dear,” She said. Your mama needs a break for a few
days.”
A huge grin broke out across Nisha’s face.
“Yes, yes…” she whisper-shouted, throwing her arms around her mother.
The next morning.
A storm broke at breakfast.
“A woman going abroad alone? With no men with them? Rahima’s mother-
in-law set down her cup so hard the tea jumped.
“What will people say? Who will cook? Do you expect me to die without
eating? You know I can’t eat when strangers cook for me.” Mrs. Akhunessa
shouted as her face started to get red.
“And who will protect you?” She said,
“Protect her from what, dadi? Nisha asked. ”Cherry trees?”
“Don’t be smart.” Her uncle, summoned by phone, arrived by noon and
delivered his verdict from the sofa.
“In our family, women do not travel without a man. ”Your father, your
brother, your husband, someone. It is not safe. It is not done.”
Rafiq sat quietly, studying the floor. He was a man who had never been
asked to choose, and so had never learned how.
“Rafiq,” his mother shouted. “Say something.”
He looked at Rahima. For the first time in years, he really looked at her. She
saw the question in his eyes, and she did something she had not done in
thirty years of their marriage. She answered before he spoke.
“I am going,” she said. ”I would like your blessing, but I am going.” Rahima
said this, finally finding the courage to have something for herself.
No one breathed.
“I have fed this family for thirty years,” she said. Her voice shook, but she
did not stop. I have never asked for anything. I am asking now. One trip.
Ten days. I will come back. I only want to see something before I am too
old to see it. And Nisha will attend her interview, and if everything goes well
, she will attend her university in Japan.”
Rafiq said nothing. But that night, she found him standing at their room
door. ”Pack some warm clothes, “ he mumbled.
”I heard it's very cold these days. I will hire someone to help around the
house while you and Nisha are away. And I will return home as early as
possible. Don’t worry about us. Then he left with a somber look on his face.
Rahima almost said that he didn’t have to worry that she would not go, but
in her heart she felt that if she didn’t go this time, the next time wouldn’t
come.
On the day of the flight, the airport felt like another planet. It was her first
time at an airport. Rahima clutched her passport and her bag tightly. A
new one, issued only last month. She had stood in the passport office in a
line of strangers, and a clerk had called her name aloud: Mrs. Rahima
Akhter. She had felt the sound of it all the way to her toes.
Nisha squeezed her hand,” Breathe, mama.”
At the time of immigration counter, a stern officer flipped through their
documents. Rahima’s heart was racing fast. She feared that if something
went wrong, then everything would go wrong.
The immigration officer glanced at Rahima, then at the space beside her,
then at Nisha.
“Where is the male guardian ?”
“Excuse me ?” Nisha said.
“Her husband, her son, a brother, someone.” He tapped the counter. “A
woman of her age, travelling with a young girl of her age with no male
guardian. This is irregular. I need to see a no-objection letter from her
husband, at least.”
Behind them, the queue murmured. Rahima felt the old dread in her chest
again, the instinct to lower her eyes, apologize, retreat to the kitchen of
herself. Her face burned. She almost turned around.
Then she remembered the window. The cherry blossoms.Her own name in
capital letters.
“Officer,” She said in a quiet voice.
He looked up, surprised that she had spoken.
“I am a forty-year-old woman. I am a citizen of this country. This is my
passport, in my name. This is my visa, in my name. This is my ticket,
bought with a daughter’s hard-earned money, in my name. The reservation
of our hotel, everything the rules mentioned in there ” Her voice was steady
but it treambled when she said.” Which law says I need a man’s permission
to leave my own country?”
The officer opened his mouth. Closed it. As if he was too stunned to say
anything.
Nisha stepped forward, calm, as if she had reheashed this in the mirror.
And truth be told, she had kind of expected this to happen, and she had
practiced it that morning. “Sir, we checked the immigration rules carefully.
There is no requirement of a male guardian for an adult woman with valid
documents. If there is a specific regulation you are referring to, we would
be glad to read it together.” Nisha almost shouted so that their
conversation could be heard at least at the back of the line.
A long awkward pause. The queue had gone silent. An older woman at the
back of the line, carrying a worn-out bag, said loudly,
“What are you thinking, Sir ?. Let them go.”
At the same time, a young man around the same age as Nisha said,
“Let them go, sir. You are also making us late for our flight.”
A few people were seen with their phones up; someone clapped softly but
then stopped, embarrassed.
The officer cleared his throat. He looked again at the passport. He looked,
perhaps for the first time, at Rahima himself. A woman with a faded pink
sari under her coat, holding her belongings in her two hands.
He stamped the page.
“Safe journey, madam and miss,” he said, a little stiffly.
“Thank you,” said Rahima. And then, because she could leave:
“Please do your job by the law and not by what people will say.”
With that, she and Nisha started to walk,
“Mama, great line. You were like a superstar; I’m so proud of you.” Nisa
said. You should have looked at his pale face.”
In the plane, Rahima’s seat was by the window.
When the plane lifted, Dhaka started to disappear into a quilt of lights, and
her whole life disappeared with it, the kitchen, the arguments, the careful
rules. She pressed her forehead to the glass and cried, quietly, without
shame.
Nisha took her mother’s hand,” Are you scared?”
“Terrified,” Rahima laughed, wiping her tears, ”And happy. I didn’t know you
could be both at the same time.”
“I know, right? I am also scared; I'm afraid the university won’t grant me the
scholarship, but I am so happy that you are going with me .”
“Even if you don’t get the scholarship, you are still my daughter. I know
would achieve great things in life in whatever you choose to do, Don’t be
too scared, dear.”
Five days later, in a park in Tokyo, the cherry trees were in bloom, exactly
like the photograph she kept hidden, except warmer, softer, and alive.
Petals drifted onto Rahima’s shoulders and into her hair. She stood under
them for a long time.
Her phone buzzed. A message from Rafiq: Send me a photo, please.
She smiled. She took one photo of the trees, and after a moment's
hesitation, turned the camera around and took one of herself. And she sent
it.
Behind her, Nisha shouted, Mama, let’s go. I am hungry.”
Putting the phone away, she took some of the fallen petals in her hand and
said ” Coming, dear.” Rahima put those petals in her bag and
smiled. THE END
