Dear Mama,
Perhaps, you never realized the sheer amount of pride I feel looking at you. Perhaps you never
noticed the sparkle in my eyes when I see you laughing. Not a pretentious one, a genuine bubbly
one. A laugh that comes from your heart. Loud and uninhibited. As if nothing in the world
matters, except for that moment.
Perhaps you never realized that I notice. I notice your exhaustion. I notice your endless passion
for work because you have us to take care of. I notice your attempts at brushing your pain, your
struggles off with a smile.
"It's a temporary world, forgive those who have wronged me," you say, but I notice.
I notice your struggle in sharing those painful stories even after years, because those are
permanent scars. They never faded; you just learned to live with them. You learned to give
yourself time and accept the hurt, but you chose to forgive those people time and time again.
I know why you do it. I know you want us to forgive them the way you have, because your heart
is made of gold. Because in every universe, I know for a fact, that you'd pick us over everything
if it meant having to go through the same struggles repeatedly.
But, you don't understand, do you? The things you've done for us, the way you've raised us is
incomprehensible. It's utterly impressive. You worked day and night, and made sure to provide
us with everything we needed and more. You showed endless patience and care towards us, even
when we asked the stupidest questions.
You were exhausted after working all day, yet you still came home and gave us time, you still
talked to us for hours, just so we didn't feel neglected. Yet, you still found the time to make
meals for us because you know how dearly we love your handmade food.
There is so much you have done for us, mum. Do you really think we would be able to forgive
those who have hurt you deeply? So much so that your breath still hitches when you attempt to
share the memories of those days with us, because those wounds were deep.
Even though the scar has healed, it can never fully disappear.
Do you really think I would see that and feel an ounce of empathy for those people, mum?
I wish you understood the strength of your presence beside me.
You bring warmth and positivity to those who know you. You have managed to show up for us
countless times. As a matter of fact, you have managed to show up as a daughter, as a sister, as a
wife, and as a mother countless times. You buy little trinkets for the children just to see their
giddy little smiles and feel the warmth of their excitement.
Every smile, every hug, every laugh of yours fills my chest with warmth, with tenderness. They
cause my heart to overflow with adoration that exists all for you.
Only if you knew.
To me, there will never be anyone whom I admire more. Not only for their resilience, but also for
their authenticity and kindness. For their bottomless pit of love for family.
What would I ever do without you, amma? Do you even realize that?
Do you even realize that I couldn't live without the warmth of your voice and the security of your
arms?
You probably don't, but that's okay.
I'll keep loving you with my entire heart 'til my end comes.
Nothing will ever compare to your affection for us.
Allergic to Emotions
The recent books I’ve been reading feel clinical, emotionless, and utterly robotic—as if the
humans who wrote them have never experienced the power of humanity, of emotions and
feelings. It seems like they have never experienced what it is to feel joy, grief, or anger.
Instead, there’s a rigidity to literature nowadays, as if writing is a chore. Not a passion project,
not a career, but something to finish within a deadline. Except that literature is not meant to be
this way.
Creative freedom exists. There is no limit to what you can write. There is a vastness, a literal
abyss for literature. No rules, no instructions. You live by your own ideas, your own designs.
Schools have a habit of teaching young learners that vocabulary matters most in composition.
You need to expand your vocabulary. Use big and complex words. Words that other people need
to Google just to understand the meaning. Use big and complex words for simple things because
people
need
to know that you have an impeccable vocabulary.
Except that is not it.
Literature is a form of art.
To be a writer, you need to have creative literacy.
It does not mean you can’t have a good vocabulary; you just need a balance. People confuse
sophistry with an impeccable vocabulary. You can sound sophisticated and impressive to other
people and still sound humane.
As a human, you need to be able to show your humane factors in your writing. You need to be
able to show your flaws, your emotions. You need to be able to express and articulate if you want
to sound humane. That is the literal definition of creative literacy.
I read a few pages of a book that a middle-schooler wrote; kudos to her, it's a big feat. However,
using complex words for the most basic of things frustrates me. I know how to write formally,
too. But we are humans. Humans have emotions. Being overly formal strips away the layer of
emotion, the humane factor.
To be a writer is to have the ability to relate to your audience.
Show resonance, show humility.
When we read books, we want to feel a connection, a bond between ourselves and the characters,
and perhaps the author too. We want to feel the emotions they are feeling, feel the grief, the pain,
the joy, whatever it may be; we want that bridge of attachment and correlation. We crave that.
A perfectly structured sentence is stripped of its layer of humanity, scrubbed of all flaws. When
the grammatical structure and the writing format are strictly formal, it starts to feel stuffy and
pretentious at one point, because it feels like your point is to show off your expanded vocabulary.
It feels like you have built a wall between us; you let us listen to a certain extent, but you never
let it get personal.
There’s no intimacy, no shared warmth.
It feels like we’re intruders in a story we had no right to know about.
The Paradox of Pride
While people might argue that pride is just simple stupidity and overestimation of one’s prowess, I will stand firm
against this claim. Pride is not always a show of idiocy, but sometimes the cloak behind unprecedented power. In my
opinion, pride can be utilized in a way that displays split-second decision-making, correct judgment of a foe’s
strength, and calculated taunting to throw off the opponent’s focus.
Pride manifests itself in many forms. In its brilliant forms, it appears as confidence, self-respect, dignity, ambition, and
determination. These aspects of pride inspire people to overcome adversity, pursue excellence, and stand firm in the
face of overwhelming odds. However, pride also possesses darker manifestations. It can emerge as arrogance,
vanity, hubris, contempt, stubbornness, and delusion. When left unchecked, these forms of pride blind individuals to
their flaws and convince them that they stand above all others.
When utilized in the right way, pride becomes the key to utter dominance. Battles don’t start physically. Intelligent
individuals break down the opponent psychologically before the true exchange of blows or the battle of wits even
starts. Dismantling the opponent’s mental defenses before the battle causes their confidence and focus to rapidly
decrease. This in turn, causes them to blunder due to rage and loss of control over their emotions. In circumstances
like these, the brilliant side of pride is shown.
For example, the Lion’s Sin of Pride, Escanor, from the anime of Seven Deadly Sins, perfectly expresses the brilliant
and good side of pride. By taunting his enemies and pitying them, he makes them lose their focus. This causes him to
utterly dominate every fight and save his fellow sins.
On one hand, one can boast to be overly prideful on the outside, causing his foe to underestimate him, while showing
his true hidden strength in crucial moments where the enemy becomes overly confident of his dominance. On the
other hand, one can use pride to pity and enrage his enemies, causing them to make arrogant mistakes and lose
their focus.
Another great representation of the brilliant, but cold and calculated side of pride is Sosuke Aizen, from the anime of
Bleach. By using his superb intelligence, he coldly predicts the strategies and moves of his enemies in a calculated
and slightly prideful nature. This overwhelming control over his opponent’s moves causes them to lose their
confidence and act wildly, which leads to utter defeat for them.
However, pride is like a double-edged sword. It can also be the cause of downfall for some. On one side, pride can
assist an intelligent individual. But on the other side, in the hands of impudent fools, it destroys them from the core.
The greatest danger of pride is that its strengths and weaknesses originate from the same source. The confidence
that allows a person to stand above others can also blind him to his own flaws. The belief that grants one courage in
battle can transform into arrogance when left unchecked.
One of the most common ways giants lose to underdogs is because of their overwhelming pride and arrogance,
which they express in it’s raw form. In turn, their uncontrolled form of pride acts as a poison against them.
A great example of this side of pride is Frieza, from the anime of Dragon Ball Z. Frieza’s overwhelming confidence
and pride prevents him from learning from his mistakes and use new strategies to defeat his opponents. He
frequently underestimates his foes, believing himself to be always above them. This is the very thing that causes him
to lose over and over again, in vain.
Too much pride blinds a person and strips them of any of their senses. It causes them to be unable to reason, accept
losses and always overestimate themselves. It also makes them incapable of admitting their failures, and preventing
him from recognizing his mistakes and learning from them.
The best example of the foolish side of pride is Kira, better known as Light Yagami, from the anime of Death Note. He
used to be a highly intelligent student who was living the high life till the death note appeared one day. Slowly, the
thought of him having the power to decide the fate of anyone made him increasingly more prideful. At one point, he
even began to think of himself as a god, which leads to his superiority complex. Eventually, his pride and God
complex leads to him being destroyed by himself due to his own arrogance and mistakes.
While I will affirm that pride isn’t always perfect and good for each and every person, I will also not deny the ingenious
sides of pride. Even as the part of a deadly sin, pride is sometimes the reason of victory and the lighter that keeps the
fire burning in one’s heart. Escanor, despite being the embodiment of one of the seven deadly sins, pride, he was
able to use his prowess and pride for the greater good of humanity, overpower the demon clan, and save his friends.
This leads to him ultimately sacrificing his life to eradicate the demon clan and save his fellow sins. With his absolute
coldness and genius level intelligence, Sosuke Aizen calmly defeats his foes without breaking a sweat by predicting
their moves and making them lose their hopes.
This is the reason pride is a fascinating trait, which ignites the fire of one’s heart, while at the same time, slowly
destroys another from the inside. Pride amplifies a person’s belief in himself. In moderation, this creates confidence,
determination, and resilience. In excess, it becomes arrogance, delusion, and self-destruction. Thus, pride itself is
neither a blessing nor a curse; it merely emphasizes the qualities already present within a person.
Yet, perhaps the matter is not that simple.
Why is pride considered a vice and sin by society, when, it is the fuel that keeps the fire inside the hearts of great
people burning? Why is pride so socially and morally condemned, when, it is the driving force behind the feats and
achievements of world class innovators, rulers, athletes, scientists, scholars and even tyrants? If one takes the time
to wonder and dwell upon these thoughts, one can eventually realize, the initial question might not be the actual one.
The initial question of pride being good or bad might not be the true one. Perhaps, beneath the multiple layers, the
true question might be whether one can control pride so it remains a servant to its master, or does it at one point,
always become the one who controls, the master even.
At the base, pride usually grants one confidence, determination, resilience to pursue almost impossible tasks. It starts
off as the driving force behind enormous achievements. Gradually, success follows one after the other. But, the path
of pride might not always be linear. At one point, pride starts blinding the master of his senses, clouds his judgement,
and eventually strips him of his common sense even. Before one realizes it, the driving force and servant that once
pushed one to success, later becomes the very thing that becomes the new master and starts controlling the path of
that person, and eventually leads him to utter failures.
So, from this observation, one can realize that pride posseses a very peculiar nature, that is unlike any other ordinary
tool. A knife doesn’t become sharper or duller because a master or beginner uses it. A pen does not become more
clever or dumber because a intelligent individual or a foolish person wields it But, pride directly amplifies the true
nature of a person, beyond the surface nature. The effect of pride entirely depends upon the wielder. Pride does not
just amplify the user’s strengths, it also amplifies the user’s weaknesses. So, fools grow dumber and wise people
grow wiser. Meanwhile, leaders may have more control and confidence, while tyrants may become grow increasingly
blinder to their flaws.
Ultimately, pride is not dangerous because of its base nature of being neutral towards all at first. It’s dangerous
because it grows with the user. The true query is not that pride might be evil or good or both at the same time, the
real question, beyond deep layers of thoughts, might be whether the user can control it to a point of keeping it in
check, before it starts becoming the very thing that controls the original wielder.
But, this is not the end of this fascinating topic. As, in my opinion, many layers remain unexplored due to its sheer
depth. Pride is basically a rabbit hole full of endless paradoxes and questions that remain unanswered till yet, leaving
philosophers delving into this topic to search for deeper layers and answer the obscure, unanswered questions.

Who Speaks When No One Wrote It?
Imagine you read a short poem on a quiet morning. It has four lines. It describes a grandmother’s kitchen after
the power goes out, when the only light comes from a pot of rice steaming on a gas ring:
“The rice keeps steaming after the power is gone,
and my grandmother counts the spoons by feel,
the way she once counted us when we were small,
so that no one is left in the dark.”
The last line makes you stop and read it again. You feel something close to grief, the good kind that makes you
want to call a parent or a sibling. The poem seems to know what it is like to love someone who is getting older.
Well, what if no person wrote it? What if a language model produced it in a few seconds after someone typed a
short request? No grandmother counted spoons. No child was counted. No kitchen existed, and no power went
out in a particular year that someone still remembers.
So ask what changed. The words are the same words. The rhythm is the same rhythm. Your eyes moved across
the same lines in the same order. Yet something seems to have left the poem. You might feel a little cheated, or
you might feel nothing at all and wonder why you ever felt anything. Either way, the poem is now a different kind
of object. The real question is who was speaking when the poem spoke to you, and whether anyone was there to
speak at all.
Roland Barthes argued that the reader is the real place where a text finds its meaning. Machine-written text seems
to fit his argument perfectly, because it appears to have no author standing in the way. But I want to argue that
this is a mistake. Barthes freed the reader from the author, but machine text removes the author without freeing
anyone. A reader cannot judge a text whose intention belongs to nobody. The missing author does not give the
reader power. It takes away the one party who could be asked to answer for what the text claims.
Roland Barthes published “The Death of the Author” in 1967. It is a short essay, and it is one of the most cited
pieces of literary criticism of the twentieth century. Its target was a habit of reading that was common in schools
and in journals. Critics would read a novel or a poem and then go looking for the author’s life to explain it. If a
poem seemed sad, the critic would find the poet’s sad years. If a novel seemed to hide a secret, the critic would
dig through letters and diaries for the secret’s source. In this approach, the author was the key that opened the
text. Once you knew the author’s intention, you thought you knew what the text meant.
Barthes thought this approach was wrong. He wrote that a text is made of many writings, drawn from many
cultures and set in conversation with each other. Its meaning does not come from a single origin. In his words,
“the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author.” This sentence is the center of the essay,
and it is often quoted without its context. Barthes was not claiming that real writers do not exist or that their lives
are useless. He was saying that the writer’s intention should not be the final judge of what a text can mean.
He also gave a positive idea in place of the old approach. He wrote that “the unity of a text is not in its origin but
in its destination.” The text gathers its unity at the point where it is read. A reader brings memory, expectation,
and mood to the page. Two readers of the same poem may find two different poems, and neither is wrong. For
Barthes, this was a kind of freedom. The reader is no longer a passive student taking dictation from a master. The
reader becomes an active maker of meaning.
Barthes also described writing itself in a way that matters here. He said that writing is “the destruction of every
voice, of every point of origin.” The text is a surface where many sources meet and none of them governs the
whole. He wanted critics to stop searching for a hidden owner behind the words and start paying attention to the
words and to the reader who receives them.
This is an idea worth taking seriously. It asks the critic to be humble about claiming to know what the writer
meant. It also gives more room to readers who come from different backgrounds and see things the author never
imagined. Barthes did not want to shut down interpretation. He wanted to open it.
The case for machine text begins with that same picture of writing as a surface of many sources. A large language
model is trained on a huge body of human writing: books, articles, forum posts, letters, product descriptions, and
poems. When it produces a new text, it draws on patterns from all of that material. The output is, in a plain sense,
a tissue of quotations drawn from countless places. Barthes used that exact image for literature. A machine seems
to be the purest case of it.
The machine also seems to have no intention in the way a human writer does. When you read a poem written by
a person, you can wonder whether the poet was sad, angry, bored, or trying to impress a teacher. Those questions
matter to the old way of reading, and they can distract from the text. With machine text, those questions have no
clear answer. There is no inner life to consult. There is no biography to check. The reader is left alone with the
words. If Barthes wanted the text to belong to the reader, machine text appears to hand it over completely.
Consider how often this situation now arises in ordinary reading. A person searches for a recipe, a medical
explainer, a product review, or a news summary and finds text that reads smoothly and sounds confident. There
is no name at the top that the reader recognizes. There may be a site, a logo, or a byline that belongs to no real
person. The reader is free to take what the text offers and fill the gap with their own sense of what it means.
The concrete examples are not hypothetical. In early 2023, the technology site CNET was found to have published
dozens of financial explainer articles written with the help of an automated system. Several of those articles
contained factual errors, and CNET later issued corrections on many of them. Later that year, Futurism reported
that Sports Illustrated had published product reviews under author profiles with invented names and stock photos,
where no real reviewer appeared to exist. In both cases, the texts were read and believed by ordinary people who
had no way to find the person who had stood behind them. The texts were free of an author in one sense, and the
readers were left without a way to check them in another.
Seen this way, machine text appears to be the completion of Barthes’s project. It has no author to block the reader,
and it offers the reader a field of meaning with nothing in the middle. The reader seems to gain the freedom that
the critic in 1967 wanted to give them. This is why the case is attractive. It is the death of the author without any
ceremony, and it looks like progress for the reader.
The French philosopher Michel Foucault answered a version of this argument only two years after Barthes. In a
lecture given in 1969, later published as “What Is an Author?”, he agreed that the author should not be treated as
a simple source of meaning. But he added something Barthes did not stress. He argued that the author is not only
a person who writes. The author is what Foucault called an “author function,” a social role that controls how texts
are classified, shared, and trusted.
Foucault gave a sharp description of this role. He wrote that “the author is the ideological figure by which one
marks the manner in which we fear the proliferation of meaning.” In other words, a society that has many possible
readings of a text uses the author’s name to narrow them. The name tells us which texts belong together, which
ones are serious, and which ones are dangerous or false. The author becomes “the principle of thrift in the
proliferation of meaning,” as Foucault put it. Without some limit, meaning would spread in every direction, and
no one would know what to believe.
Foucault’s point is easy to see in ordinary life. A medical leaflet with no company name, no doctor, and no date
would not be trusted, even if the words were clear and accurate. A scientific paper without authors or institutions
would be hard to cite. An anonymous legal notice would be ignored by most people, and rightly so, because a law
needs a source that can be identified. In each case, the name is not just decoration. It tells the reader what kind of
text they hold and how much weight it should carry.
This means that readers still depend on something outside the text when they decide what it means and whether
to believe it. They look for a name, a publisher, a purpose, or an institution. When the name is missing, they look
for another way to place the text. The reader does not stand alone with the words. The reader stands with a set of
assumptions about who would produce such a text and why.
Machine text does not remove this need. It only removes the name that would normally meet it. So the reader
begins to look for a substitute. They may trust the platform that displayed the text, the website that published it,
or the company that built the system. They may assume a human editor checked it, even when no editor did. They
may trust the tone of the writing, which is often calm and sure of itself. These are weak replacements for an
author, and they can be wrong. But they show that the author function is still working, even when no author exists.
Foucault therefore gives a sharper version of the problem. The death of the author did not end the social role the
author played. It only left that role empty. When the role is empty, the reader must fill it with guesses, or they
must accept whatever the machine offers.
Here is my position. The missing author does not free the reader. It leaves the reader with no one to hold
responsible for a claim.
Barthes’s reader is a reader of pleasure and play. A poem can mean many things, and the reader can enjoy the
variety. But many texts are not poems. A text can say that a medicine is safe, that a bridge was inspected, that a
candidate took a bribe, or that a historical event happened on a certain date. These are claims about the world. A
claim is a kind of promise. It says, in effect, that someone stands behind these words and can be asked why they
are true. When a text makes a claim and no one stands behind it, the claim is still on the page, but the promise has
nobody to keep it.
This is the difference between reading for pleasure and reading for trust. In a poem, a missing author costs us a
little. We may enjoy the text anyway. In a news report or a medical explainer, a missing author costs much more.
The reader cannot ask the writer what the source was. The reader cannot ask whether the writer checked the
number. The reader cannot press the writer to correct a mistake or punish a lie. The reader can only accept the
claim or reject it, usually with very little information.
Responsibility is not a cold bureaucratic idea. It is the mechanism that makes trust possible. A journalist who
signs a story can be questioned, corrected, challenged in court, or dismissed for dishonesty. An editor who
approves a story takes on part of that responsibility. A reader who sees the name of a reporter they have trusted
for years has reasons to believe the story, because they know who would pay a price if it were false. Trust is built
on a chain of people who can be held to account. Remove the people, and the chain breaks.
Machine-written text breaks that chain in two places. The first is the writer. The system that produced the words
cannot be questioned in any meaningful way, and it cannot feel shame or accept blame. The second is the
publisher. A publication that uses machine text may not disclose it, may not check it carefully, and may not own
the errors in the way a human writer would. The CNET corrections show what happens next. The errors were
fixed, but the reader who had already acted on a wrong explanation had no one to hold accountable for the harm.
The fake reviewers in the Sports Illustrated case were not even a real person who could later say what they had
tested.
This matters most in journalism. A news story is only useful if the reader can judge how it was made. Was the
source a government report, a rumor, or a guess? Did a reporter speak to the people involved? Did an editor
review the claim? A machine text can imitate the surface of a news story without any of these steps. Its fluent
sentences look the same whether the facts are checked or invented. The reader is left to guess, and the guess is
made harder by the very smoothness of the writing.
Education is another place where the missing author causes damage. When a teacher reads a student’s essay, the
essay is evidence of what the student understands. The teacher asks whether the argument is the student’s own,
whether the sources were read, and whether the student can defend the claims in conversation. If the essay was
produced by a machine, the evidence is false. The teacher cannot judge what the student learned, and the student
has not learned what the grade says they learned. The essay is a text with no one behind it who can be asked to
explain it. In this case, the death of the author does not free the student. It takes away the process that education
depends on.
Some will say that these are problems of bad actors, not of the text itself. A dishonest writer can always lie,
whether a human or a machine. That is partly true. But the old system of authors, editors, and names gave readers
a way to tell honest work from dishonest work. It was imperfect, and it failed often. Still, it gave readers something
to check. Machine text, used without disclosure, removes that check from the reader’s hands. It makes the lie
harder to trace and easier to repeat.
So I do not think readers should celebrate the death of the author as a simple gift. Barthes was right that a reader
makes meaning, and right that a text should not be closed by a single intention. But a reader who makes meaning
from a claim about the world still needs to know where the claim came from. The reader should not be freed from
this question. The reader should be given a harder duty, which is to ask who stands behind the words, what they
would lose if the words were false, and how the claim can be checked. Barthes’s reader cannot do this alone. They
need institutions, names, and a clear line of responsibility, even if those things are imperfect.
Return now to the four-line poem about the grandmother and the rice. On the first reading, it moved me, and I
think that reaction was real. The image of a family in the dark, held together by a counting that is almost a prayer,
is powerful. Nothing in my argument changes that the lines work on the senses and the feelings. Barthes would
say that the poem still belongs to me, and that my feeling of grief is the meaning it has for me now.
But the argument does change how I read the poem. When I learned that no one wrote it, the grandmother stopped
being a person who once counted children in the dark. She became a character invented by a system that had
learned how such images are usually built. The line “so that no one is left in the dark” stopped being a moment
of love and became a pattern that moves a reader. I can still enjoy the pattern, and I may still feel something when
I read it. What I can no longer do is treat the line as a sincere statement from someone who knows what it costs
to keep a family together. There is no one to ask what the line meant to them, and no one who would stand behind
it if it were false.
That is the loss the missing author leaves behind. Some pleasure may remain, and I do not think that pleasure is
worthless. But trust does not move with the words. Trust needs a person, and a person needs to be answerable.
When the author is gone and nothing takes the author’s place, the reader is alone with a claim that no one will
answer for. That is not freedom. It is a kind of abandonment, and the reader should see it clearly before accepting
the words at face value.
To lean to the light
Sometimes when the curtains are drawn and the Sun sets to sleep, I remember my
Mumma.
I’ve lost many past memories; they’ve turned into a liquefied slurry of sceneries and lights
and faces, swirling around and sometimes dribbling a drop or two into my mind, where it
results in nothing but confusion as I try to recall the full picture in vain.
But Mumma…my Mumma I remember. I feel it would be impossible to forget.
In the morning, when golden beams manage to spill through a gap or two between the
blinds and cut bright wedges around me, an equally brilliant image of her pops in as well:
the way sunlight poured through her canopy to cast various aureate shapes around me,
serving as my playmates for the day.
She was beautiful in all different ways I can imagine, not only the way her viridescent
leaves and weeping aerial roots drooped to the ground like a newly-wed’s veil, but also how
she stood her ground, how her vast trunk with the millions of ridges and furrows it had
gained throughout the years protruded from the rough soil into the open sky, enormous
snake like roots meandering their way across the surface, anchoring her in place. My
Mumma was the most magnificent of them all, the queen of that peaceful little patch of
forestry I was born in amidst the bustle of urbanization.
I was only a tiny sprout swaying in between two massive distributary-like roots, peeking
through my mother’s leafy awning to get a glimpse of the glassy blue sky above. They would
often mistake me for a mere weed, and I didn’t mind, as long as Mumma herself
acknowledged me. She would ruffle her leaves and breathe into mine, saying that I would
grow, grow just like her, higher and mightier, even, until I could touch the clouds, that I
would become the heart of this place we lived in. “Just lean towards the light, “ she advised,
as rays poked through her leaves, “Lean to the light, and it’ll do the rest.”
At first it was just me, and Mumma, and the other plants who called her their queen. Then
came she, one fine autumn morning, as my mother parted her aerial roots and I saw my
baby sister. At dusk, when Mumma’s branches would be crowded with those tittering birds,
we would participate in their lively conversation. Sometimes, a bird or two would
tentatively fly down to the damp ground, reach out, and as we conversed, they’d carefully
pick out the miniscule bugs and ticks nestled under our leaves.
Sometimes, now, when the occasional sparrow comes to rest on the veranda, I chuckle at the
memories of those chirpy friends of mine.
My Mumma liked to tell stories, stories of her life and the things she’d seen, heard, felt. Me
and my sister would dedicate our full attention to her as she recounted her time as a
maiden tree, and how the loud city around us was once a serene countryside.
Mostly, we loved hearing accounts of ‘The People’. “They’re magical creatures.” Mumma
would muse. “They do unimaginable things, some giving life while others take it away.”
The first time I saw “The People” was when I was quite a few months old. They looked like
bamboo sticks merged on a trunk to make five branches, the top one small and getting more
rounded, with a bush atop. They came in different sizes and shapes, like us trees, and they
wore different colors of skins over their trunk and branches. It was peculiar, really.
They came and flashed their flat little devices, making snapping sounds across the
plantation. Mumma stood rigid as they uttered enthusiastic remarks.
I could only catch on to one tiny snippet of it, one I can recall to this day: “The Queen
Banyan”.
When they left, I could tell by her features that she was worried about them returning,
despite her assurances. In contrast, Sister was practically bubbling, chattering to the birds
and our neighbours about “The People” in her usual vibrant tones.
Mumma was right. They did return. And that’s what made me who I am today.
It was a winter, dry and flaky. Instead of the dense white envelope of fog, the sky was a
sickly grey, streaks of black particulates cutting their way through before showering dust
on the canopy. Then all broke loose. Soil crumbled and dust flew, clogging my senses as the
very earth trembled uncontrollably. I only caught a glimpse of those huge ‘machines’,
bounding in, the noise overwhelming me as it overlapped the shrieks of my neighbours. I
flailed around for Sister, and spotted her place amongst the pandemonium…but she wasn’t
there. Gone. Uprooted and flattened by the rollers of the machines. I gazed up at it, and
saw someone behind the screen. “The People”.
The same ones who fascinated my baby sister so much.
And all Mumma could do was stand there, holding her ground, as one of the monstrous
things approached.
I don’t remember the rest, and I’m glad for that.
The next thing I can recall is rumbling and lurching and pitch-black darkness, a darkness
so consuming it tried to swallow me whole. I think there was a small sliver of murky light
from some corner, but the dark swallowed that too, before gnawing at what now remained
of me.
Then it faded.
I was somewhere else, lined up along with hundreds more of others. It was a humid, fuzzy
atmosphere, the air heavy with a mixtured scent of different flowers, damp soil, fertilizer,
manure, rainwashed bricks, and so much more. All around me were different versions of
me, small and weak and slowly ebbing away. Our roots roughly dug into the crumbly, dry
soil filling plastic container. More of those ‘People’, as they took us from place to place,
ripping, digging, ripping again.
My Mumma. I wondered where she was.
It faded again.
Someone called me that. The one they called my Mumma. “Banyan”. It sounded nice. Like
home.
I was somewhere else again.
Roots loosely anchored into the caky soil.
Another word. “Bonsai”.
I wondered what that meant.
Someone was gently fingering through my leaves and branches. I caught a glimpse of his
face. One lined with experience. Like Mumma.
The next few days, months maybe, or perhaps years, went like a fast forwarded collection of
reels. I was grown alongside a row of similar plants, in round sepia tobs, surviving on water
that smelt of wrought iron.
We, the lined tobs of plants, never felt very inclined to share our stories. Perhaps because
we didn’t remember it. Perhaps we didn’t want to.
I knew I didn’t.
I wondered where Mumma was.
There was one thing, though. There was light. I remembered what Mumma said.
“Lean to the light.”
So I obeyed.
But then it was gone.
I was in a different place. Colder and dimmer.
I had learnt another term. “Human”.
There he was, the one with the lines in his face like my mother’s.
His gnarled, calloused hands were soft and gentle on me.
For a split second, I felt hope.
Snip.
And a
crunch
and a small thud as one of my branches landed at my roots.
Why?
Snip again, and again, until it was joined by more, my leaves and branches which had just
seen the light.
Then came the wires.
They curled around what remained of me like the snakes that used to come out during
monsoon, wrapping and bending and binding. Splints all over me.
I had become better at understanding them. Humans. They said I didn’t feel the pain.
Which must be true, I didn’t even know what pain meant.
But I wished it would be over. I wished I could go back to Mumma, stay in her shade, listen
to her stories. Lean to the light. There was barely any now.
More cutting, wiring. They called it pruning. Said it made me beautiful.
Aesthetic
Needles. Needles and syringes, piercing the loose soil into my roots. I wondered what they
did.
All I had to do was grow. That was it. Grow. Hold my head up high into the sky, like
Mumma. Then they couldn’t keep me anymore.
But, I didn’t. The tiny sprout by the porch had become quite large now. But I hadn't. I was
still here, in my sepia tob.
I still am now.
They come to see me. Call me beautiful. A natural wonder.
But not with the awe that made their eyes glow when they saw my mother.
I was different. Beautiful, aesthetically pleasing, yes. But not
natural.
Not my mother.
They try, but they can’t hide that unease from their eyes.
I don’t blame them.
They have a new word for me now, “Bonsai”.
Light is pouring through the window now. Inviting me.
Lean.
I try. I really do. But I can’t.
I hope Mumma understands. She always did.
I love you.
Silence
Abontee Ahmed
Oh Silence! You are the essence of me. You are the veil upon the face of my Beloved. The worst
trait of silence is that through it, fear and hope vanish. If a human remains silent before his
destiny and utters no complaint, he will have neither fear nor hope.
Before Allah destroys me with sorrow and grief, He will not grant me the treasure hidden within
me. Before He carries me away with a burning flood, He will not lead me to the sea of wisdom. I
am a mirror.
I am a mirror. I am the one who is talkative and distracted. Because I am silent, you do not hear
the cries of my heart. Would that your ears could turn into eyes, so you might see how helpless I
am.
I am like a tree shaking its hands in the wind. I orbit like the moon in the sky. When I am upon
the earth, my orbit carries the scent of soil. I am the color of dust; yet though I am made of dust,
since I hold a sacred spirit within, my orbit is purer, more beautiful than the orbit of the heavens.
O Silence, you are my essence. You are my face.
O Sage, speak! Speak, that I may pray for you; for you speak the truth. For every dawn, when the
time of prayer arrives, I become more beautiful, joyful, exultant, and intoxicated.
So upon myself I swear, I shall never deprive you of my warmth or mirth.
And I ask God that whatever He has decreed for the possessor of my heart, He may grant half of
it to me.
The cup of Truth and the cup of Eternity, the Beloved Himself has given them to me. The beggar
who drinks from that wine becomes a fountain of the sun, a divine light giving drink to the
thirsty.
My throat is parched; I can no longer speak.
I have fallen silent.
O sage of beautiful speech, O dweller of my heart, O star of my joy, speak to me, for you are the
possessor of a voice like Dawood’s (AS.) and I am as a mountain uprooted and ruined by divine
command.
Abontee Ahmed

I believe there's a kid that lives inside everyone. A kid shaped by their environment, the way
they were treated, talked to, cared for. That becomes their default image. No matter how
much their life changes, how many storms they pass through, that is how they see
themselves.
You cannot erase that child. Whether that's a good thing depends entirely on which child you
got.
For some, it's beautiful. They were given the affection they needed during their critical years.
They grow up carrying that image of themselves: happy, carefree, without a second thought.
Now let's come to the ones who didn't have it.
Constantly criticized. Constantly made to feel bad about themselves. Constantly neglected.
What does the kid inside them do?
They become exactly what they're told.
You're not worthy of love.
I'm not worthy of love.
You're forgettable
. I'm forgettable.
You're not wanted
. I'm not wanted.
They grow up too, like any other human. Carrying that child inside them, along with the
words they heard and believed to their core.
And they grow to be…
Wait. Did you think I'd talk about the meek, quiet ones? The ones who never learned to raise
their voices against anything that tries to oppress them?
Well, they exist too. I'm not ignoring them.
But we'll keep them aside for today.
Let's talk about the ones who grow up to be dangerously confident. Who don't seem to care
even if the grim reaper appears in front of them. Who'll carry an entire debate with him, too,
and with unbelievable ease.
Sometimes people look at them and think: where does all that confidence come from?
People admire them. People want to be like them. Compliments are not new to them.
These people are magnetic as hell. There's something that draws others toward them,
something they can't quite pinpoint. But it's addictive. So addictive they can't stop.
So the kid is healed, right? It's getting everything it wanted. Praise. Affection. Attention it
deserved.
You think confidence cured them?
Wrong.
It just learned to wear a different face.
Here's a little thing about confidence. People see it as a magical drug, something that
miraculously cures every negative thought, every criticism you believe to be true about
yourself. You achieve it and voila, insecurity isn't part of your life anymore.
As if you haven't carried these thoughts, these voices, these tears for ages. As if it's that
easy to undo years of psychological pain.
And external validation is of no help. Sure, it can momentarily lift one's spirit. It can even
make someone's day a little better.
Key words:
Momentarily. Day.
That kid? It still feels the same.
The Strangers I Knew
Prologue

I have never travelled by myself anywhere, certainly not somewhere as far as Beanibazar. When you come from a sheltered family like mine, travelling with company is always a must, at least a pair of two. Yet, here I was, preparing to journey to my ancestral village. My
dada bari.
On my own. For the first time.

I shall admit, I was surprised when I first found out about the plan. My dad being the strict and protective man that he is would never let his daughter travel by herself. He never let any of my four elder sisters either, yet here I was. What has changed?

I stared at the back of my father’s head as he scrolled through his phone while reading different articles on our country’s situation. My father, Harun, has always been very good at hiding his emotions. True emotions to be exact. And by emotions, I mean, I have never seen him cry. Being the short-tempered man that he is, I have seen his fits of rage, and I have seen him smile. But the only time I heard about him genuinely being happy was when my eldest sisters, Sharmin and Shumin were born. Perhaps it was the excitement of having his first children, but the stories I heard of the man he was then resemble nothing to the man I know him as. Almost as if they are different people.

Not to forget, those were stories I heard from my mom, not him. My father has never been the talkative one with his children, let alone make idle conversations. True, he has always done his duties as a father, fed us, clothed us, educated us, raised us. Everything a father was meant to do. But I can’t remember the first or last time I had a decent conversation with him.
Kun shomoi baraoi bai?
(When will you leave?)” My mother asked from the kitchen, walking into the room and placing a cup of milk tea before my father without turning her attention to me, but I knew she was addressing me.
Ou baroi zaimu
. (Just in a bit.)” I replied, watching her gracefully roam around the room before perching like a docile bird across from my father.

She was… rather good at concealing her inner thoughts. She, Fathima, always had a smile on her face, but she did have her moments of rage if we were unruly. However, I could never tell what she really thought now and then, and it made me wonder if she ever thought at all. My mistake, she did think; about Ahmed. Her only son.
A lot.

Ahmed was my mothers greatest joy, just like Shireen, my third sister was father’s greatest pride. They may have felt the greatest when they had their first two children, but the favorites were their third and fourth- Ahmed and Shireen. As for my fourth sister Tarin and myself being the last, I wasn’t sure.
I didn’t know what they thought of me.
The baroi zao ekhon. Baade der oizibo.
(Then you better leave now, lest it becomes late.)” Were my father’s words to me, barely looking up from the phone in hand. But I could sense the concern edged in his voice.
I’m sure they loved me, but sometimes I can’t help but wonder if I was something they considered a gift, a choice, or a responsibility.
I pursed my lips before getting to my feet, smiling at them. “
Acha.
(Okay.)”
Because when you have a total of six children, the excitement of parenthood already disappears by the time the third or fourth child is born, let alone the sixth child.
Turning to look at my parents sitting across from one another, I knew exactly what they were.
The textbook versions of parents.
To be on Your Own

Starting from Shaporan I hailed an auto rickshaw that drove me till the bypass road, from where I then hailed yet another auto rickshaw that took me further inside only to drop me off at Gulapgonj. Every time I finished a trip, I found myself releasing a sigh of relief knowing that I was getting closer and closer without getting abducted or harassed. A girl can never be certain.

Yet, my journey was far from over, but close nonetheless. I was close to Narafing, and from here on, I could travel via manual rickshaw, which was the part I was looking forward to the most. Riding a rickshaw all by yourself with the wind brushing past your face as it speeds by was a welcoming thought, especially when it was the rural breeze of nature.

Epilogue

“Aicho ni? (You came?)” My mother’s voice was the first to greet me when I got back, but I said nothing, watching as she placed plates on the table for dinner while my father washed his hands to eat. It was him next. “Khaar goro khailai? (Whose house did you eat?)”
I replied to them after that. We ate, and they asked me mundane questions, and I replied. Like every other day. Only it no longer felt like every other day.
I look at my father, as if looking at him for the first time.
The boy who dreamt to be a doctor, to study medicine and then travel the world. To taste new things, and buy his mother pretty sarees.
Only that you never become one.

You never became a doctor, Harun. You never study medicine. You don’t travel the world, and you don’t really taste new things. And you see very less of your mother in the coming years before she passes away.

Fate had other plans for you, and it had nothing to do with the war that would follow the very next year after I saw you. You will grow up to become a bright young man, a pride of your mother and sisters. But not in the way you imagined.

You will travel to UAE because life in Bangladesh had nothing for you. But life in UAE ends up delivering more obstacles than you expected. Still, you fight through. You fight through, and you marry my mother. And you have us.
The dreams of the little boy from 1970 are pushed far back in the corner of your mind because keeping your new family thriving becomes your first priority. The sacrifice of a father.

I then turn to my mother. The girl who was once so loved and cherished by her parents, protected and sheltered. The girl who knew nothing beyond her pretty clothes and dolls and the rhymes sung to her. The ever-carefree child who grew up too fast.

Sooner than later you have a sister, and your parents will play favorites, until you are no longer the little girl who knew nothing beyond her pretty clothes and dolls and the rhymes sung to her. You become the shield that takes the blows for your siblings, the job of the eldest child. And over time, you experience as the shield child curves you into being the wife people expect you to be, a mother the generation deems a perfect fit.
And then you have us, and like father, we become your world. Like your siblings, we become the one in need of a shield. The sacrifice of a mother.
They all grew up too fast. The lines in their faces tell that story.
Somewhere along the way, youth left you behind, and we were born. We became your world, your priority. Being parents overrode the idea to be dreamers.
After all, you too, were just children with dreams, like us.

And perhaps it does not excuse the feeling of depravity of love that I felt as your child, or the reasons why you had favorites. It doesn’t explain why you could ask you other kids about their day and never mine until I was the last person left at home. Or why my presence in the house was always compared to that of my siblings. Never too much, never enough.
But it probably explains why you both are the way you both are.
You may not have fulfilled your childhood dreams, but you became the perfect parents.
So, now that I look at you, I know a little more.
The perfect mother and father. But not mom and dad.
And I guess, that is alright.
For there is no saying what future has in store for me too. If I too, will be expected to grow up fast. If I too, will be forced to push my dreams behind and become a responsible adult.
So, I guess, it is fine.
It is alright.
I know parts of you, and you know parts of me. But we can never know everything.
We are all strangers to one another somehow. Strangers that we know.

The Record and the Choice
The coin in your pocket, a planet in orbit, or the wheel of your childhood bicycle,if you take
the distance across that shape (its diameter) and around it (its circumference), then divide
that circumference by the diameter, you will undoubtedly land on
π
However, this is not a math lesson.
π
is more than just a string of decimals that your teacher
tells you to round to
on a random Tuesday. It is a storage of every piece of information
humanity has ever come across. With its infinite decimal numbers that never repeat into a
pattern, it is said that it holds every possible combination of numbers. Thus, somewhere in
the depths of the digits of
π
lies your birth date, your phone number, and the exact moment
of your greatest achievement. More surprisingly, if those numbers are converted into letters,
it holds the exact words of every lyric sung, every word ever uttered, and every book ever
written.
That would mean that the very words I am typing right now, or the thought I will form in a few
moments, already exist, sitting quietly in the infinite decimals of
π
Perhaps this means that the story of my life, your life, or simply what I am going to eat
tomorrow is all written in
π
. Now the question arises: if the map of my entire life was drawn
before I even drew my first breath, does that mean my choices aren’t really mine?
Okay wait, let me ask another one: this means that the next movie everyone is hyped about
and the score of tomorrow's match are all waiting quietly in
π
, even the lyrics of the song that
keeps popping up on your "For You" page every other day. Why write the script anyway, or
why spend so much time thinking about the perfect words for the article that you will have to
publish tomorrow?
I know I am getting a bit out of hand, because although this information exists, it certainly
does not in the first 100,000 digits of
π
. And since it is infinite, you can’t really tell where it
exists. However, as technology emerges and advances, I assume it won't be very difficult to
continue calculating many digits of
π
and thus find such information.
Now, even if finding it is impossible, let us take a hypothetical situation where we know all the
digits of
π
. This would mean that somewhere in there is every scrap of information you could
possibly find. Does this mean that my whole life isn’t really mine, or maybe I shouldn’t even
bother writing this article, because somewhere in the digits of
π
, there is everything I will ever
think, say, or do,so... what even is the point?
The answer lies in the fact that a record of what will happen is not the force or action that
makes it happen. In the infinite digits of
π
. There are also every other variation of my life: one
where I fail the test, one where I skip breakfast, and one where a single digit of my phone
number is altered. Therefore, even if a supercomputer does find all the digits of
π
, I wouldn’t
know whether a given sequence is my actual life or just a false variant.
If I choose to study today and get good marks on my test, that specific reality exists in the
digits of
π
. But if I choose not to study and fail, that outcome is also sitting somewhere in
π
The record exists because I choose it, not the other way around.
The Pale Lunar Horizon
Mikhail adjusts the volume of his headset till it drowns out the tinnitus. Music really helps
keep inspections like these vaguely within the bounds of being tolerable. Without the music,
Mikhail is certain he would have lost his mind within the first week. He does so with one
hand, careful to keep the other firmly on the steering wheel; the rover does not have great
traction, and he would rather not get stuck out here. The scenery is desolate, oppressive
even. It’s almost an assault on his senses, yet he presses on through the endless stretches of
the featureless grey dust.
His shift is nearing its end; just two more sites and he can finally turn back to base. Mikhail
slows down the buggy as he approaches the penultimate destination on his list, another one
of those aging radio telescopes. Recently there’s been quite a bit of chatter about this
particular telescope back home in Moscow. Some anomalous signal or some such. But
Mikhail, for one, couldn’t care less. He was a pilot before
Lunokhod,
not a scientist, and all
this astrophysics business almost made him want to go back to appreciating the lunar vista,
or its lack thereof.
The rover slides to a gentle stop. Mikhail unstraps himself and gets off the vehicle with the
generous assistance of the aft pallet. Even after a month, the suit and the gravity still mess
with his head, making it tedious to even complete the simple act of standing still.
Nevertheless, he’s slowly acclimatizing. Leaving behind the rover, he bobs himself over to
the concrete reflectors, all to the melodious tune of
Swan Lake
. After an optimal sweep,
satisfied with his findings, he begins his trod back to the buggy.
The music glitches. A few mangled notes drag themselves for a second before cutting off
entirely, leaving Mikhail alone with only the dull sound of his own breathing to accompany
him. “
What the...?”
he mutters, tapping on his visor, trying to figure out what just
happened. He is met with deafening silence, not even static.
Mikhail decides to hail the operator before it gets too suffocating. “
Zvezda, do you read?”
he begins,
“I think there’s some radio interfere-
", but he never gets to finish.
He’s in the rover, driving towards the observatory, the pale lunar horizon in front. He slams
on the brakes, bringing the vehicle to a halt. “
What in the name of the Ever-Loving God just
happened?!
” he asks the vacuum. He doesn’t hear an answer. Not that he expected to hear
one; that would’ve been horrifying. But still.
For a solid minute, he simply stares into the abyss where the sky generally is back home. He
checks with his instruments and with Zvezda; no, he really is back on the rover. After a bit of
deliberation, Mikhail convinces himself that he had just dozed off and dreamt up the whole
ordeal, albeit in an unnaturally vivid manner. He chalks it up to his isolation and embarks on
his course anew.
Everything seems to be going swimmingly; he reaches the observatory, disembarks, and
begins his inspection of the telescope. That is until the music starts to break up again. He
feels a sinking sense of déjà vu as he slowly turns towards the reflector. And in that
moment, the realization hits him like a speeding train. He was not dreaming. Greeting
Mikhail was an entity that he could only describe as the manifestation of incomprehensible
dread, a quasi-physical nightmare he couldn’t articulate into words even if he tried. He feels
a chill run up his spine and grip his chest, smothering him like the silence around him. He
tries to breathe, but his lungs seem suddenly unwilling to cooperate. His muscles scream at
him to run, but it’s as if he has forgotten how to. Mikhail freezes, paralyzed by the
overpowering presence and his brain’s incapacity to process what was before him.
He’s in the rover, driving towards the observatory, the pale lunar horizon in front. Mikhail is
now positively petrified. The music is back again, but he can barely hear it on account of his
heart drumming in his ears. He contemplates escape and jolts the rover around,

He’s in the rover, driving towards the observatory, the pale lunar horizon in front. Mikhail

I. The oil pastels
Squeezed into the plastic box, they stay there, behind the sheaf of papers, cracked files and old books.
Some tall and proud despite fading colors, some stubbed and wedged painfully at the feet of others,
some with their covers peeling and adorned with a mass of networking scribbles, and others
fairly…alright, they huddle there in the dark like refugees in a camp.
They’ve been like this for a fairly long time, waiting for the sudden bursts of instances where they sensed a
slant of light over their plastic home, felt the wretched walls before them being stirred and moved over to
the side as the plastic box was pulled out.
For the first time in a while, the lid would be turned and they’d see light, and a wonderful view of the
cracked ceiling above. They would be selected to show themselves off on a thin sheet of paper, a task they
completed very eagerly indeed. And even as they’re placed back into the dark, the excitement and utter
pride of the ones who were selected would provide enough fuel for life for the days to come.
And so they sit there, more or less patient, for the only one who had the power to grant them this long
awaited momentary freedom. The only one who could crack the rigid walls before them and let them see
light.
So they wait, and they wait for her.
How much longer?
II. The plastic cup
Holding on to the arm of the metal stand, it watches as the next batch is taken to the sink.
There’s plates, pans, saucers and bowls, alongside glasses and cups just like itself, waiting their turn to be
doused in the cold water. Some of the cups send fleeting glances of pity, while others remain rigid, their
backs turned to it.
It remembered back when it used to be part of this batch, participating in merry clacks, clitters and thuds
into the bustling conversations that took place at the sink. Everyone had complaints about their use: being
too rough, using too much oil, using too less, being ruthlessly stashed into the rack, jumbled up with others.
It itself never took part in this, it never had to. It liked the touch of the small, warm fingers of its user curling
around its handle, the sloshing of water to dissolve the orange juice powder at its bottom, the soft sips, the
noisy ones with the following burst of cheeky laughter, the unicorn and barbie stickers smothered over its
surface.
For some time now, though, it’s been hanging from the rack, relieved of its duties. This happened sometimes
of course, for a whole month once, but she always returned, sometimes bringing a new sticker to take its
place on the pale orange surface.
Yes, that must be the case, it thought as it watched the water gurgling over the others at the sink.
Yes, that’s it.
Then why wasn’t it taken to the sink?
And what was this throb it felt, as if something else had happened?
III. The schoolbag
Stashed under the table, it counted footsteps. Footsteps of the people coming into the room, going out.1, 2,
Just 14 footsteps today. From three different people. Far too less. It could be wrong. The lights barely
came on at night, and it had to rely on sound. During the day, it seemed to be just the maid, dragging the
broom behind her. It could be wrong. It probably was. It felt more tired now, slumping here against the
dimness. Fully packed, it felt the load of the books and copies inside itself, neatly slotted according to
period, the pencil case reigning in its separate pocket. The tiffin box was there too, for a while, until it was
taken out a while ago, leaving the water bottle behind. It would be a Tuesday, then, according to the
arrangement of the books.
Then why weren’t they taken out?
And why has it been here, for so long, instead of its daily place beside her desk at school?
It was confusing. And so tiring, being here, with nothing to do but counting the footsteps. The steps that
were clearly diminishing in number.
And where was the playful slapping of the bright pink slippers against the tiled wall, the sound that woke it
up from its trance everyday? The infectious laughter, the recitations from the books it contained?
It all felt so…misplaced. So wrong.
It didn’t understand. Where were all the sounds?
IV. The books and the lamp
Something’s been different.
Different from the usual difference, that is.
They watch as, all of a sudden, the room’s abuzz with activity. Briskly sweeping brooms, washcloths being
dragged across the tiled floor, corners of the ceiling being dusted, the film of dust being wiped off the
books. As the lamp was hoisted up and had a rag wiped over it, it exchanged glances with the three
books lined along the table to be next.
For the first time in ages, they felt a brewing excitement. An excitement originating from the unspoken
question on their minds: Was she back?
Presently, they took their respective positions on the study desk, the lamp with its craning neck, the books
expectant.
Yes, something was definitely different.
As dusk started smothering the sunlight, the lights were turned on.
The already made bed was made again, the windows glossed over once more.
The curtains were drawn.
The next time the door opened, someone came in.
Someone who hadn’t ever been in the room before.
The lamp braced itself instinctively, and the books below it, blindly following despite their lack of vision,
did the same.
He flipped through some of them, placed them back. The lamp was turned on, once, and put out again.
Hushed, snippets of words were passed.
Everyone around him stood rigid, too rigid really, like a brick wall shielding the ruins of a reign.
There were some more words, of gratitude, sorrow, promises.
Another book was picked up, flipped through. The lamp remained switched off.
When the door opened again, and he left, they looked through again, eagerly. Would she come in now?
She would, right?
The books looked up to the lamp again. Well?
The lamp tried to look further through the door, to catch a glimpse. Just one.
The day after, everything was the same again. The days were silent, the nights were dark. A room like a
soundless corpse.
They exchanged looks again. Well?
V. The calling bell
Unlike many others, it was used.
It felt lucky for that, at least.
Every few days, sometimes consecutively, someone would lay their finger’s weight on the switch, and it
could clear its voice to call out.
The switch assumed superiority here, as if it were a means of control. The rest of the circuit went by its
whims.
For some time now, though, the switch had been quiet. The circuit was glad of that, but they didn’t
understand why. Perhaps it needed to be replaced again.
This was often the case. Except this time.
The switch was guilty.
It was guilty of what its pride made it think was a crime.
The crime of being a witness.
That day, a Tuesday morning as the calendar above the shoebox suggested, it had been a witness.
The girl had just come out, letting the bright pink sandals fly off as she strapped on her school shoes.
She was humming to herself, it remembered, tuned words chirping under her breath. This was a daily sight,
of course, and the switch itself paid mind to only scrutinizing her for all the noise she made.
Then the door opposite opened. The switch wasn’t paying much attention, and it barely noticed what
happened next.
There was a woman.
There was the girl, one school shoe still in hand.
She was standing now.
She took a few steps, one after the other towards the other door.
A pink sandal trailed behind her, as if beseeching her not to go.
The last thing the bell saw was the swish of her dark hair as the door of the other apartment closed behind
her.
It wondered afterwards, when all the other people gathered in front of that door, amongst the hammering
fists and the screams and cries, whether it could’ve done something. The singular slipper, powerless and
forgotten, sitting silently beneath it, looked up once.
You saw,
it said.
You saw.
Could it have done something? If it tried, if it really had tried, perhaps it could wake the circuit up to call
out. That was its job, wasn’t it.
If it really was in control, it could’ve called out.
It could’ve made sure the girl came home one more time, one more time she could’ve jammed her little
fingers onto the switch for it to call out.
VI. The school gate
It didn’t really have much to say.
Nothing changed for it much.
The students still came in, went out. Hundreds of them. It couldn’t count.
Students holding their parent’s fingers, students fixing their skirts and ponytails, heaving their books,
laughing and gushing with friends.
There was no difference.
No difference at all.
No difference at all, as one sister came in through the gates, leaving the other behind.
VII. The People
They didn’t understand.
Like the pastels, or the plastic cup, the stashed away schoolbag, the loyal lamp and the books, the bell
switch, and definitely the school gates, they didn’t know.
No matter how much they read about it on social media, how many posts they reacted to, how many
heartfelt comments they left behind, they didn’t understand.
You can’t blame them. Some things are left incomprehensible in this great, civilised, knowledgeable and
advanced world.
Perhaps these things are best left that way. Perhaps not everything is to be comprehended, and that’s how
we manage to forget the absolute horror that happened to a girl, put a cover over it, and call the next
day a peaceful one.
And we move on. And, well, those who can’t, they are left behind to sit before what lies beyond that cover.
We talk of justice, we shed a few tears, listen to words sprinkled around by the ones in power, smother
newspapers with a child’s face who should never have that headline beneath her picture, and perhaps, in
the least, are shaken by the fact in the dead of the night that such things are actually possible and
repetitive on this Earth.
And a child who’s biggest fear should be the huge spider they saw crawling away under the cabinet, faces
something our brains don’t even have the capacity to fathom.
And so, the world remains as it is behind its veil of peace.

The Tale of The Mediterranean
People love that word. Illegal. Illegal immigrant. Illegal border. Illegal boat. They say it with
clean mouths, in clean rooms, over clean water. Nobody says illegal hunger. Nobody says
illegal poverty. Nobody says illegal childhood without food.
The sea doesn’t care about any of that. It just swallows.
Salt water burns my throat. Behind me, a child is choking—crying, maybe praying. It smells
like vomit and sweat and fear. The sky is too beautiful tonight. Stars everywhere, silent, far
away. The sea glitters even while it kills. I hate how beautiful it looks.
The stars make me think of her.
I’m back in that government hospital. Stained walls. A fan creaking like it might fall. Patients,
nurses, pain. Then she cried, and none of it mattered. I held her like she was glass. I
promised her safety. I had no right to promise that. She wrapped her fingers around mine
and I felt ashamed. When she smiled the first time, I thought I’d seen heaven.
I took the bracelet home from the hospital. It’s been in my wallet since. It’s wet now. I keep
touching it.
After she was born, I worked and counted money. Somehow it was never enough. Her
clothes grew smaller, and I kept telling myself things would get better. They didn’t. I sold my
land. I sold my mother’s jewelry. I can still see the empty box. I sold my dignity piece by
piece until all I had left was this journey. I paid for a seat on a boat that shouldn’t be floating.
It’s full of men like me. Not criminals. Not monsters. Just fathers who ran out of options.
The world loves a sacrifice story. Noble. Beautiful. Make a movie about it. But when we
actually do it—when we actually risk our lives—they call us illegal. They want our sacrifice to
stay poetic. Not real.
The boat rocks. Someone screams. Someone prays. Someone throws up. The smell of
death gets stronger. Like death is already here, sitting with us, waiting.
I count my days. Maybe hours. I keep thinking about her face. I can’t remember the exact
sound of her laugh anymore. That scares me more than the waves. I’m scared I’ll die without
remembering her right. I’m scared my love won’t be enough to keep her safe. I’m scared I’ll
get to Europe and still fail her.
The sea doesn’t answer that either.
If I live, maybe she’ll grow up where she doesn’t know hunger. She’ll learn a language I can’t
speak. Wear clothes I can’t afford. Laugh at things I’ll never understand. And maybe one day
she’ll forget me. Let her. If she sleeps warm, if she eats, if she grows up without fear, I won’t
ask for anything more.
Another wave hits.
I close my eyes. I see her. Her fingers around mine. Her first smile. The warmth of her
against my chest. I wish I could hold her one more time. The water rises. I try to hear her
laugh, but all I hear is the sea.
Will she remember me?
Then it goes dark.
The tale of the Mediterranean will go on...
I just hope she knows I tried.

Touch Me Not

It was back in 2013, when I was in class four that I first met Babul sir. He was my Islamic studies teacher. I remember the first time he saw me, and how he never looked away, not until he was already in his seat, and one of my classmates was asking him what he’d teach us today. Babul sir ignored him entirely. His very first words were, “We have a new beauty in our class!”
I instantly knew who he was talking about, not just me, but everyone present. I was the new student after all. Did his compliment make me feel flustered and shy? No.
I was unnerved.

Not because all attention was on me then, but because of the look in Babul sir’s eyes. Something about the way he watched his new student felt primal and unprofessional. The way his eyes never left me even as he asked me to stand up and introduce myself despite the fact that I had already done so in the first period, and the way his sleazy eyes scanned my every move. It was… disgusting.

Now, here I was, five years later, watching the man as he exited the administration building, or more like the principal’s office after receiving his expulsion notice. With his head bowed, he avoided eye contact and scurried out like a little sewer rat. But this time, my eyes never left him.

Apparently, some students from junior classes had reported him for sexual assault, not one or two, but many, and when the complaints kept piling up, they decided it was time to let this long-standing faculty member go, that is if they wanted to protect the school’s image. I knew those girls. They were in fourth grade, same as when I was. Some of them had sisters in my class, which was why news travelled quickly to me. Turns out, Babul sir had become quite bold over the years.

From watching female students and unnerving them, he had moved on to even touching them, holding hands, placing them on his lap, and what not. All in the name of ‘Teacherly affection.” Or sometimes, “Fatherly figure”. I didn’t know father’s affections were supposed to be this uncomfortable.

The little girls who filed the complaints came rushing to our class to inform their sisters about the good news, and I remember the joy in their faces.
